literature.lead_zh: 本期埃博拉病毒类群研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 暴发 在遏制方面表现出了重大挑战,其快速增长归因于响应延迟和有限的 监测 能力。 [10.1080/22221751.2026.2744490]
在 4 名具有强 GP 转录 (GP Ct 1,2 IgG) 的患者中检测到了 sGP 并进行了定量,但在 GP 转录较低 (Ct > 25) 的患者中未对其进行定量,无论其抗埃博拉病毒 GP 1,2 IgG 结果如何。 [10.1128/jvi.01414-26]
审查得出的结论是,与 埃博拉病毒 相比,Ervebo 对 Bundibugyo 病毒病的保护作用可能受到 Bundibugyo 抗体识别率低 2.8 倍的影响。这表明,Ervebo 疫苗接种 后对本迪布焦病毒的抗体反应可能高于基于 埃博拉病毒病 数据的推定保护阈值。 [10.64898/2026.10.02.26364627]
确诊病例从 8 例增加到 2073 例,确诊死亡人数达到 796 例。覆盖范围扩大到五个省份的 45 个卫生区。有条件的六个月情景差异很大,预计到 2027 年 1 月 14 日累计病例数将在 2435 例至 10,839 例之间。 [10.3390/v18101104]

2014-2016 年西非 暴发 最初在几内亚报告,随后传播到利比里亚和塞拉利昂,仍然是迄今为止记录的最大埃博拉病毒病 暴发,病例数超过 28,000 例,死亡人数 11,308 人。由不同正埃博拉病毒属引起的疾病分别被指定为埃博拉病毒病 (EVD)、苏丹病毒病(SVD)、本迪布焦病毒病(BVD)和塔伊森林病毒病。“埃博拉病”一词是对由不同正埃博拉病毒属引起的疾病的广义称呼。 [10.4274/mjima.galenos.2026.261007]

papers.title: Early Action Review of Detection, Notification, and Response Timeliness during Cross-Border Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak, Uganda, 2026.
papers.abstract: Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), an Ebola virus species with no licensed vaccine or therapeutic, reemerged in May 2026 as a cross-border outbreak in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. During a 2-day workshop, July 8-9, 2026, we conducted an early action review of the outbreak response using the 7-1-7 framework (7 days to detect, 1 day to notify, 7 days to complete early response actions) to assess timeliness and identify bottlenecks and enablers across 9 response pillars. Uganda declared its outbreak on May 15, 2026; by July 8, the country had recorded 20 confirmed cases (15 imported, 5 locally transmitted) and a case-fatality rate of 15%. Uganda met all 3 targets: detection in 6 days, notification in <1 day, and response completion in 2 days. Low clinical suspicion, cross-border data-sharing gaps, fragmented digital systems, and delayed community engagement were common bottlenecks; strong leadership and coordination structures were most cited enablers.

papers.title: Predicting the efficacy of Ervebo against Bundibugyo virus disease
papers.abstract: There is currently no clinical data for the effectiveness of the only licensed Ebola virus disease vaccine (Ervebo) against Bundibugyo virus disease. A number of studies have shown immune cross-reactivity with Bundibugyo virus after Ervebo vaccination. However, antibody recognition of Bundibugyo is around 2.8-fold lower than recognition of Ebola virus. Here, we aimed to infer how a 2.8-fold drop in immune recognition may affect Ervebo protection against Bundibugyo virus disease based on analysis of data on Ervebo immunogenicity and protection from Ebola virus disease. This work has three main components. Firstly, we analysed the timing of vaccine protection in the Ervebo pivotal ring vaccination clinical trial. Secondly, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of antibody responses to Ebola virus after Ervebo vaccination over time. Thirdly, we combined these data with previously reported data on the cross-reactivity to Bundibugyo virus to infer protection of Ervebo against Bundibugyo virus disease. We find that the clinical trial data for Ervebo supports vaccine protection beginning earlier than 10 days after vaccination. Secondly, binding antibody levels against Ebola virus on day 28 post vaccination (peak responses) were on average 12.9-fold (95% confidence interval, CI: 6.4 - 26.0) higher than on day 7, 6.3-fold (95% CI: 3.7 -10.8) higher than on day 10, and 2.5-fold (95% CI: 1.4 - 4.4) higher than on day 14 (neutralising antibodies showed similar results). Finally, we consider the scenarios where antibody levels to Ebola virus at day 7 or 10 are putative protective thresholds against Ebola virus disease, and we assume these thresholds also apply for Bundibugyo virus disease. Then, with a 2.8-fold reduction of responses to Bundibugyo compared to Ebola virus, we predict antibody responses to Bundibugyo virus after Ervebo vaccination are likely above these putative protective thresholds.

source_records.abstract: There is currently no clinical data for the effectiveness of the only licensed Ebola virus disease vaccine (Ervebo) against Bundibugyo virus disease. A number of studies have shown immune cross-reactivity with Bundibugyo virus after Ervebo vaccination. However, antibody recognition of Bundibugyo is around 2.8-fold lower than recognition of Ebola virus. Here, we aimed to infer how a 2.8-fold drop in immune recognition may affect Ervebo protection against Bundibugyo virus disease based on analysis of data on Ervebo immunogenicity and protection from Ebola virus disease. This work has three main components. Firstly, we analysed the timing of vaccine protection in the Ervebo pivotal ring vaccination clinical trial. Secondly, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of antibody responses to Ebola virus after Ervebo vaccination over time. Thirdly, we combined these data with previously reported data on the cross-reactivity to Bundibugyo virus to infer protection of Ervebo against Bundibugyo virus disease. We find that the clinical trial data for Ervebo supports vaccine protection beginning earlier than 10 days after vaccination. Secondly, binding antibody levels against Ebola virus on day 28 post vaccination (peak responses) were on average 12.9-fold (95% confidence interval, CI: 6.4 - 26.0) higher than on day 7, 6.3-fold (95% CI: 3.7 -10.8) higher than on day 10, and 2.5-fold (95% CI: 1.4 - 4.4) higher than on day 14 (neutralising antibodies showed similar results). Finally, we consider the scenarios where antibody levels to Ebola virus at day 7 or 10 are putative protective thresholds against Ebola virus disease, and we assume these thresholds also apply for Bundibugyo virus disease. Then, with a 2.8-fold reduction of responses to Bundibugyo compared to Ebola virus, we predict antibody responses to Bundibugyo virus after Ervebo vaccination are likely above these putative protective thresholds.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on predicting the efficacy of Ervebo against Bundibugyo virus disease. The central question is how a 2.8-fold drop in immune recognition of Bundibugyo virus compared to Ebola virus may affect Ervebo's protective capacity against Bundibugyo virus disease. The topic boundary is limited to human-pathogenic orthoebolaviruses, with Bundibugyo virus and Ebola virus as the primary targets.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review includes a systematic analysis of Ervebo's immunogenicity data from the pivotal ring vaccination clinical trial, a meta-analysis of antibody responses to Ebola virus over time, and a comparison with previously reported cross-reactivity data to Bundibugyo virus. The methods involve examining the timing of vaccine protection and quantifying antibody levels at different time points post-vaccination.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that Ervebo's protection against Bundibugyo virus disease may be influenced by the 2.8-fold lower antibody recognition of Bundibugyo compared to Ebola virus. It suggests that antibody responses to Bundibugyo virus after Ervebo vaccination are likely above putative protective thresholds based on data from Ebola virus disease.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review acknowledges that the evidence for Ervebo's efficacy against Bundibugyo virus disease is limited to inferred data based on cross-reactivity and immunogenicity studies of Ebola virus. There is no direct clinical data on the effectiveness of Ervebo against Bundibugyo virus disease, which creates an evidence gap.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review highlights the need for further research to directly assess Ervebo's efficacy against Bundibugyo virus disease. It also suggests that future studies should focus on understanding the protective thresholds for Bundibugyo virus and validating the assumption that these thresholds are similar to those for Ebola virus disease.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the potential efficacy of Ervebo, the only licensed Ebola virus disease vaccine, against Bundibugyo virus disease. However, the lack of direct clinical evidence for Bundibugyo virus disease remains a significant gap. The findings imply the need for further research to directly evaluate Ervebo's protective capacity against Bundibugyo virus disease.

papers.title: Ebola virus disease through the one health lens: Integrating human, animal and environmental health for preparedness, prevention, and control – A narrative review
papers.abstract: Ebola virus disease (EVD) is a severe, often fatal zoonotic disease that continues to pose a serious public health challenge, especially in Central and West Africa. Despite major progress in diagnostics, infection prevention, vaccination, and therapeutics, Ebola outbreaks repeatedly reveal gaps in surveillance, preparedness, ecological risk monitoring, and community trust. The disease is not driven by the virus alone; its emergence and spread are shaped by interactions between wildlife reservoirs, environmental change, sociocultural practices, population movement, and fragile health systems. Viewing EVD through a One Health lens helps in understanding these connections more clearly. Human health, animal health and ecosystem health are closely linked, and Ebola prevention cannot depend only on clinical care after cases appear. Effective control requires early detection of human illness, monitoring of wildlife and ecological risks, strong laboratory systems, infection prevention in health facilities, timely treatment, safe and dignified burial practices, vaccination where applicable and meaningful community engagement. Risk communication must be based on trust, respect and local participation, particularly in communities where caregiving and funeral practices are deeply rooted in social and cultural life. Although recent advances have improved the outlook for Ebola control, important challenges remain. Weak intersectoral coordination, inadequate financing, limited veterinary public health capacity, insecurity, fragmented data systems and low community confidence continue to affect preparedness and response. Strengthening One Health platforms at local, national and global levels is therefore essential, not only for EVD, but also for future emerging and re-emerging zoonotic diseases in a rapidly changing global landscape.
papers.journal: Journal of Integrative Medicine and Research

papers.source_body_en: Ebola virus disease (EVD) is a severe, often fatal zoonotic disease that continues to pose a serious public health challenge, especially in Central and West Africa. Despite major progress in diagnostics, infection prevention, vaccination, and therapeutics, Ebola outbreaks repeatedly reveal gaps in surveillance, preparedness, ecological risk monitoring, and community trust. The disease is not driven by the virus alone; its emergence and spread are shaped by interactions between wildlife reservoirs, environmental change, sociocultural practices, population movement, and fragile health systems. Viewing EVD through a One Health lens helps in understanding these connections more clearly. Human health, animal health and ecosystem health are closely linked, and Ebola prevention cannot depend only on clinical care after cases appear. Effective control requires early detection of human illness, monitoring of wildlife and ecological risks, strong laboratory systems, infection prevention in health facilities, timely treatment, safe and dignified burial practices, vaccination where applicable and meaningful community engagement. Risk communication must be based on trust, respect and local participation, particularly in communities where caregiving and funeral practices are deeply rooted in social and cultural life. Although recent advances have improved the outlook for Ebola control, important challenges remain. Weak intersectoral coordination, inadequate financing, limited veterinary public health capacity, insecurity, fragmented data systems and low community confidence continue to affect preparedness and response. Strengthening One Health platforms at local, national and global levels is therefore essential, not only for EVD, but also for future emerging and re-emerging zoonotic diseases in a rapidly changing global landscape.

papers.title: Endogenous anti-Ebola virus GP1,2 antibodies interfere with detection of secreted glycoprotein in the blood of EVD patients.
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Ebola disease (EBOD) is a highly infectious disease with severe hemorrhagic symptoms. It is caused by orthoebolaviruses , which include the Ebola virus ( Orthoebolavirus zairense ) (EBOV) causing Ebola virus disease (EVD), the most lethal EBOD to humans. Through co-transcriptional polymerase stuttering and subsequent proteolytic processing, its GP gene produces multiple protein products, including secreted glycoprotein (sGP) and structural membrane-associated trimeric GP 1,2 . Although sGP is known to circulate in the blood, its physiological significance in disease pathology remains speculative. We quantified sGP using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) in 36 acute human EVD cases from the 10th and 11th EVD outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) using single-time-point biobanked samples. We detected and quantified sGP in four patients with strong GP gene transcription (GP Ct 1,2 IgG. However, sGP was not quantified in patients with lower GP transcription (Ct > 25), regardless of their anti-EBOV GP 1,2 IgG results. While two patients, MAM179 and MAM271, had notably strong GP transcription (Ct 1,2 IgG might have interfered with detection by the assay detection antibody, a human anti-EBOV GP 1,2 /sGP IgG. Furthermore, the addition of sera containing anti-EBOV GP 1,2 IgG reduced the binding between sGP and anti-EBOV GP 1,2 /sGP used as detection antibodies. This suggested that the level of sGP in circulation is strongly linked to the intensity of GP transcription. Additionally, circulating sGP in this context would form complexes with anti-GP 1,2 antibodies, hence hindering additional antibody binding for detection. IMPORTANCE Insight into the mechanism of immune function by the Ebola virus secreted glycoprotein (sGP) in humans is essential for better understanding viral pathogenesis, immune protection, and immune evasion strategies. Research utilizing samples from patients who are infected with or have survived infection with the Ebola virus offers an unparalleled opportunity to determine the immunological significance of sGP. This research evaluates, in acutely infected patients from Ebola virus disease outbreaks, the role of EBOV sGP in modulating antibody responses directed against viral entry glycoprotein. By elucidating how sGP influences antibody-mediated immunity, the study advances our understanding of a conserved immune-evasion mechanism shared across all orthoebolaviruses. These investigations are valuable resources for designing more efficacious vaccines, therapies, and biomarkers for monitoring Ebola virus diseases.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of secreted glycoprotein (sGP) from the Ebola virus in modulating antibody responses against the viral entry glycoprotein. Using ELISA, sGP was quantified in 36 acute EVD cases from the 10th and 11th outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. papers.title: VSV-EBOV vaccination induces cross-reactive T-cell responses against Bundibugyo virus in humans
papers.abstract: Abstract Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) is causing an ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) with no licensed vaccine available. Recent reports have shown the presence of BDBV-cross-reactive antibody responses in humans vaccinated against the related Ebola virus (EBOV). Here, we used an IFN-γ ELISpot assay to assess T cell responses against the EBOV, BDBV and SUDV glycoproteins in clinical trial participants vaccinated with the licensed VSV-EBOV vaccine. We could show that BDBV-cross-reactive T cell responses are detectable in the majority of individuals and that conserved regions within the glycoprotein are targeted. In the absence of a BDBV-specific vaccine, these data support efficacy trials of the VSV-EBOV vaccine during the current outbreak.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate whether the VSV-EBOV vaccine could induce cross-reactive T-cell responses against Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), given the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the lack of a licensed vaccine.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted using clinical trial participants who had been vaccinated with the licensed VSV-EBOV vaccine. The research focused on assessing T-cell responses against BDBV and related viruses such as EBOV and SUDV.
analysis.methods: The researchers employed an IFN-γ ELISpot assay to evaluate T-cell responses against the glycoproteins of EBOV, BDBV, and SUDV in vaccinated individuals.
analysis.main_results: The results demonstrated that BDBV-cross-reactive T-cell responses were detectable in the majority of individuals, with conserved regions within the glycoprotein being the primary targets.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the VSV-EBOV vaccine may offer some protective benefit against BDBV, as it induces cross-reactive T-cell responses, which is a novel insight in the context of vaccine development for related Ebola viruses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide important information for the potential use of the VSV-EBOV vaccine in controlling BDBV outbreaks, supporting the need for further efficacy trials during current outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on cross-reactive T-cell responses rather than direct viral challenge or clinical outcomes, and the evidence is moderate due to the absence of long-term follow-up data.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates whether the VSV-EBOV vaccine, licensed for Ebola virus (EBOV), can induce cross-reactive T-cell responses against Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), which is causing an ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Using an IFN-γ ELISpot assay, the researchers assessed T-cell responses against the glycoproteins of EBOV, BDBV, and Sudan virus (SUDV) in vaccinated individuals. The results showed that BDBV-cross-reactive T-cell responses were detectable in most participants, targeting conserved regions of the glycoprotein. This finding supports the potential use of the VSV-EBOV vaccine in BDBV outbreaks, although the study's evidence is moderate due to the lack of direct clinical outcomes. The research highlights the importance of evaluating cross-reactivity in vaccines for related viruses, which could inform future trials and public health strategies.

We could show that BDBV-cross-reactive T cell responses are detectable in the majority of individuals and that conserved regions within the glycoprotein are targeted. In the absence of a BDBV-specific vaccine, these data support efficacy trials of the VSV-EBOV vaccine during the current outbreak.

papers.summary_zh: 摘要 本迪布焦埃博拉病毒 (BDBV) 正在刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 引发持续的 暴发,且没有获得许可的 疫苗。最近的报告显示,接种相关 埃博拉病毒 (EBOV) 疫苗的人类中存在 BDBV 交叉反应性抗体反应。在这里,我们使用 IFN-γ ELISpot 测定来评估接种许可的 VSV-EBOV 疫苗 疫苗的临床试验参与者对 EBOV、BDBV 和 SUDV 糖蛋白的 T 细胞反应。我们可以证明,在大多数个体中可以检测到 BDBV 交叉反应性 T 细胞反应,并且糖蛋白内的保守区域是目标。在缺乏 BDBV 特异性 疫苗 的情况下,这些数据支持当前 暴发 期间 VSV-EBOV 疫苗 的功效试验。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 鉴于刚果民主共和国正在进行的 暴发 且缺乏获得许可的 疫苗,该研究旨在调查 VSV-EBOV 疫苗 是否可以诱导针对本迪布焦病毒 (BDBV) 的交叉反应性 T 细胞反应。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是使用已接种许可的 VSV-EBOV 疫苗 疫苗的临床试验参与者进行的。该研究的重点是评估 T 细胞针对 BDBV 和相关病毒(如 EBOV 和 SUDV)的反应。
analysis_zh.methods: 研究人员采用 IFN-γ ELISpot 测定来评估接种疫苗的个体中 T 细胞对 EBOV、BDBV 和 SUDV 糖蛋白的反应。
analysis_zh.main_results: 结果表明,在大多数个体中可检测到 BDBV 交叉反应性 T 细胞反应,其中糖蛋白内的保守区域是主要目标。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,VSV-EBOV 疫苗 可能对 BDBV 提供一些保护作用,因为它诱导交叉反应性 T 细胞反应,这是 疫苗 相关 埃博拉病毒 开发背景下的新颖见解。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果为 VSV-EBOV 疫苗 在控制 BDBV 暴发 中的潜在用途提供了重要信息,支持在当前 暴发 期间进行进一步疗效试验的需要。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于其依赖于交叉反应性 T 细胞反应,而不是直接的病毒攻击或临床结果,而且由于缺乏长期随访数据,证据并不充分。

papers.title: Rapid Geographic Expansion, Decelerating Growth, and Six-Month Scenario Projections of Bundibugyo Virus Disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: Analysis of Situation Reports 1–61
papers.abstract: In May 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared an outbreak of Bundibugyo virus disease caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus. We analysed aggregated official Situation Reports (SitReps) issued from 14 May through 14 July 2026 to describe the reported epidemic trajectory, geographic expansion, mortality, interval-specific growth, and conditional six-month projections. Confirmed cases increased from 8 to 2073 and confirmed deaths reached 796; 45 health zones in five provinces were affected. Average interval-specific growth rates generally declined over the observation period, although cumulative cases and the geographic footprint continued to increase. Gompertz and Richards curves described the observed cumulative trajectory better than logistic and exponential curves according to root mean square error (RMSE), the corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc), and the Bayesian information criterion (BIC); this comparison reflects in-sample fit only. Conditional six-month scenarios varied substantially across assumptions (approximately 2435 to 10,839 cumulative cases by 14 January 2027) and are contingent and highly uncertain; Gompertz fits showed underprediction of the subsequently reported total in four temporal checks. Reported case fatality ratios (CFRs) varied across provinces but are vulnerable to outcome delay, incomplete case ascertainment, small denominators, and retrospective reclassification. The results support continued surveillance and response planning but do not identify the causes of epidemic slowing or establish that transmission was controlled.

analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed aggregated official Situation Reports (SitReps) issued from 14 May through 14 July 2026, covering 45 health zones in five provinces affected by the outbreak.
analysis.methods: The researchers used SitReps to describe the epidemic trajectory, geographic expansion, mortality, interval-specific growth, and conditional six-month projections, employing statistical models to fit the data.
analysis.main_results: Confirmed cases increased from 8 to 2073, with confirmed deaths reaching 796. The geographic footprint expanded to 45 health zones across five provinces. analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the geographic expansion and growth dynamics of Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo using Situation Reports from May to July 2026. It found that confirmed cases and deaths increased significantly, with the outbreak affecting 45 health zones across five provinces. The researchers used Gompertz and Richards curves to model the epidemic trajectory, which outperformed logistic and exponential models in in-sample fit. However, six-month projections were highly uncertain, ranging from 2435 to 10,839 cumulative cases by January 2027. The study highlights the importance of continued surveillance but does not establish the causes of the epidemic slowing or confirm transmission control. The findings are of moderate evidence strength due to potential biases and limitations in the data source.

papers.title_zh: 刚果民主共和国本迪布焦病毒病的快速地理扩张、增长减速和六个月情景预测:情况报告分析 1-61
papers.source_body_en: In May 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared an outbreak of Bundibugyo virus disease caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus. We analysed aggregated official Situation Reports (SitReps) issued from 14 May through 14 July 2026 to describe the reported epidemic trajectory, geographic expansion, mortality, interval-specific growth, and conditional six-month projections. Confirmed cases increased from 8 to 2073 and confirmed deaths reached 796; 45 health zones in five provinces were affected. Average interval-specific growth rates generally declined over the observation period, although cumulative cases and the geographic footprint continued to increase. Gompertz and Richards curves described the observed cumulative trajectory better than logistic and exponential curves according to root mean square error (RMSE), the corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc), and the Bayesian information criterion (BIC); this comparison reflects in-sample fit only. Conditional six-month scenarios varied substantially across assumptions (approximately 2435 to 10,839 cumulative cases by 14 January 2027) and are contingent and highly uncertain; Gompertz fits showed underprediction of the subsequently reported total in four temporal checks. Reported case fatality ratios (CFRs) varied across provinces but are vulnerable to outcome delay, incomplete case ascertainment, small denominators, and retrospective reclassification. The results support continued surveillance and response planning but do not identify the causes of epidemic slowing or establish that transmission was controlled.
papers.abstract_zh: 2026年5月,刚果民主共和国宣布由本迪布焦埃博拉病毒引起的本迪布焦病毒病为暴发。我们分析了 2026 年 5 月 14 日至 7 月 14 日发布的汇总官方情况报告 (SitReps),以描述报告的流行病轨迹、地理扩张、死亡率、特定区间增长和有条件的六个月预测。确诊病例从8例增加到2073例,确诊死亡人数达到796例;5个省的45个卫生区受到影响。尽管累积病例和地理足迹持续增加,但在观察期内,平均特定区间增长率普遍下降。根据均方根误差(RMSE)、修正的赤池信息准则(AICc)和贝叶斯信息准则(BIC),Gompertz和Richards曲线比Logistic和指数曲线更好地描述了观测到的累积轨迹;此比较仅反映样本内拟合。有条件的六个月情景在不同假设之间存在很大差异(截至 2027 年 1 月 14 日累计病例数约为 2435 至 10,839 例),且具有偶然性且高度不确定;Gompertz 拟合显示对四次时间检查中随后报告的总数的预测不足。各省报告的病死率(CFR)各不相同,但很容易受到结果延迟、病例确定不完整、分母较小和回顾性重新分类的影响。结果支持持续的 监测 和应对计划,但没有确定疫情放缓的原因或确定 传播 已得到控制。

papers.full_text: Abstract Ebola disease (EBOD) is a severe viral illness with a high mortality rate caused by viruses of the genus Orthoebolavirus within the family Filoviridae. The emergence of a new outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in Ituri Province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo on May 15, 2026, along with the detection of cross-border cases in Uganda, has once again underscored the global public health significance of EBOD. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current terminology and classification, pathogenesis, modes of transmission, clinical and laboratory findings, diagnostic methods, case definitions, treatment approaches, Infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, contact tracing, vaccination strategies, and long-term sequelae associated with EBOD. Currently licensed vaccines and monoclonal antibody therapies are approved only for Orthoebolavirus zairense, limiting treatment options during BDBV outbreaks. Accelerating the development of pan-filovirus vaccines and therapeutics, strengthening early diagnostic capacity, and improving IPC infrastructure remain key priorities. Introduction Definition, Classification, and Current Terminology Ebola disease (EBOD) is a severe viral illness caused by viruses of the genus Orthoebolavirus within the family Filoviridae. Under the current classification, the principal Orthoebolavirus species known to cause human disease include Ebola virus (Orthoebolavirus zairense, EBOV), Sudan virus (Orthoebolavirus sudanense, SUDV), Bundibugyo virus (Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense, BDBV), and Taï Forest virus (Orthoebolavirus taiense, TAFV). The diseases caused by these viruses are designated Ebola virus disease (EVD), Sudan virus disease (SVD), Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), and Taï Forest virus disease, respectively. Thus, the term “Ebola disease” is used as a broad designation for diseases caused by different Orthoebolavirus species[1, 2]. History and Epidemiology EBOD was first recognized in 1976 during simultaneous outbreaks in present-day South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), caused by SUDV and EBOV, respectively. Subsequent outbreaks occurred predominantly in Central and East Africa, particularly in the DRC, Uganda, Gabon, and Sudan. Although the magnitude and mortality of outbreaks have varied according to viral species and epidemiological context, EBOV outbreaks have generally been associated with higher case-fatality rates. The 2014-2016 West African outbreak, initially reported in Guinea and subsequently spreading to Liberia and Sierra Leone, remains the largest EVD outbreak recorded to date, with more than 28,000 cases and 11,308 deaths. Limited healthcare capacity, inadequate surveillance systems, deficiencies in infection prevention and control (IPC), urban transmission, and extensive population mobility contributed to its rapid expansion. Travel-associated cases identified in Africa, Europe, and North America further underscored the potential for international dissemination of the disease. Recurrent outbreaks have continued, particularly in the DRC, including the 2018-2020 outbreak, which resulted in 3,470 cases and 2,287 deaths. The 2022 outbreak in Uganda further underscored the persistent public health significance of SUDV[3-5]. Mortality varies according to the causative viral species, access to healthcare, and the epidemiological and clinical characteristics of individual outbreaks. Comparative epidemiological characteristics, pooled case-fatality rates, and currently available vaccines and therapeutic options for EBOV, SUDV, and BDBV are summarized in Table 1. Overall mortality was 61.3% among patients treated in sub-Saharan Africa, compared with 24.5% among those treated outside sub-Saharan Africa[6]. Epidemiological risk is also shaped by the social context in which exposure occurs. Differences in exposure risk by sex and age appear to reflect social roles and caregiving responsibilities rather than established biological differences in susceptibility[20]. Environmental Drivers and One Health Perspective Environmental and social changes may influence both the risk of zoonotic spillover and the subsequent geographic spread of EBOD outbreaks. Changes in land use, including deforestation and other forms of forest conversion, may modify human-wildlife interfaces and increase opportunities for contact with potential animal reservoirs. A spatial analysis of 27 Ebola outbreak sites and 280 control locations in Central and West Africa found that outbreak occurrence near the margins of the rainforest biome was associated with dense forest loss during the preceding 2 years. However, this observational association does not demonstrate that forest loss alone causes EBOD outbreaks, and the mechanisms connecting environmental change, human-wildlife contact, and zoonotic spillover remain incompletely understood[21]. Following a spillover event, transport connectivity and population mobility may facilitate geographic dissemination by connecting remote outbreak locations with other settlements and population centers. An analysis of EBOV outbreaks found that the extent of road and river networks surrounding spillover sites was significantly associated with the number of cases recorded during the first 100 days of an outbreak[22]. The 2014-2016 West African epidemic further demonstrated how introduction into capital cities, extensive population mobility, and cross-border movement, coupled with weak surveillance, inadequate IPC, and strained healthcare systems, can facilitate sustained transmission and international spread[3-5]. However, the infrastructure analysis did not incorporate indicators of population density, settlement size, or urban-rural status and therefore did not directly assess urbanization as an independent determinant of outbreak spread[22]. Moreover, because the analysis included only EBOV outbreaks, these findings should be extrapolated cautiously to outbreaks caused by other Orthoebolavirus species. Taken together, these findings support a One Health approach that integrates human disease surveillance with animal and environmental monitoring while fostering coordination among public health, veterinary, wildlife, and environmental authorities. Incorporating land-use and population-connectivity data into this multisectoral framework may improve assessment of spillover risk, facilitate early outbreak detection, and strengthen preparedness. Nevertheless, evidence linking specific environmental and social drivers to Ebola emergence remains predominantly observational, and causal relationships have not been definitively established[23]. The 2026 BVD Outbreak: Epidemiological Characteristics, Public Health Response, and Lessons Learned On May 15, 2026, an outbreak of BVD was declared in Ituri Province in northeastern DRC, and outbreak-associated cases were subsequently identified in Uganda. As of July 21, 2026, the DRC had reported 2,536 laboratory-confirmed cases and 1,033 deaths among confirmed cases across Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, and Tshopo provinces. Uganda had reported 20 confirmed cases, including 2 deaths, and 1 probable case resulting in death. Fifteen confirmed infections were imported from the DRC, whereas 5 resulted from secondary transmission among contacts and healthcare workers. No sustained community transmission had been documented, and the most recent confirmed case in Uganda was identified on June 21, 2026. An imported case was also reported in France; the patient subsequently recovered, and no secondary transmission was detected. Because case investigations, laboratory confirmation, and data harmonization were ongoing, these reported figures should be considered provisional[24-27]. Reported cases accumulated considerably faster than during previous major EBOD outbreaks. By mid-July, the World Health Organization (WHO) had characterized the event as the third-largest Ebola outbreak on record and reported that approximately 2,000 confirmed cases had been identified within about 2 months, whereas the 2018-2019 outbreak in the DRC required more than 10 months to reach a comparable case count. Nevertheless, the epidemic curve should be interpreted cautiously. The rapid increase in cumulative case counts may not reflect transmission occurring exclusively during the same period, because intensified case finding, expanded access to laboratory testing, and retrospective analysis of previously collected specimens may have incorporated earlier infections into the surveillance dataset. Ituri remained the principal epicenter, although the detection of cases across five provinces demonstrated the potential for continued national and regional spread[15, 26]. The response has unfolded in a complex setting in which multiple operational challenges have compounded one another. Armed conflict, population displacement, and restricted access to affected communities have coincided with limitations in healthcare services, laboratory capacity, IPC resources, and referral systems. Community mistrust, misinformation, and security incidents involving healthcare facilities and personnel have further disrupted surveillance and response activities. As of July 15, 2026, 119 confirmed infections, including 36 deaths, had been reported among healthcare workers in the DRC. This substantial occupational burden indicates ongoing exposure in both healthcare and community settings and highlights gaps in the consistent implementation of IPC measures. Collectively, these conditions may delay case recognition, disrupt contact follow-up, compromise safe referral and clinical care, and allow transmission chains to remain undetected[26]. On May 17, 2026, the WHO Director-General determined that the outbreak constituted a Public Health Emergency of International Concern under the International Health Regulations. The decision emphasized the need for coordinated international action in response to rapid geographic expansion, documented cross-border transmission, and continuing epidemiological uncertainty. The absence of licensed BDBV-specific vaccines and therapeutics further heightened the need for research and regulatory preparedness. Vaccine candidates were prioritized for expedited development, and clinical studies evaluating therapeutic and post-exposure prophylactic interventions were initiated during the outbreak. These approaches are discussed in the relevant sections below[15, 16, 26, 28]. The public health response has focused on three complementary objectives: achieving earlier case identification and isolation, reducing transmission associated with healthcare and community exposure, and strengthening coordination across affected provinces and national borders. Measures supporting these objectives have included expanding diagnostic capacity, conducting active contact follow-up, establishing safer referral and clinical care pathways, training and protecting healthcare workers, implementing community-based risk communication, ensuring safe and dignified burial practices, and facilitating more timely exchange of epidemiological information among neighboring countries. Maintaining dedicated isolation and treatment capacity and ensuring reliable access to appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) have remained particularly important in newly affected areas[26, 29]. This experience demonstrates that standard containment measures may become less effective when delayed diagnosis, population mobility, insecurity, healthcare worker exposure, and limited health system capacity occur simultaneously. Preparedness for future outbreaks should therefore include decentralized laboratory networks that can be rapidly expanded, pre-established mechanisms for cross-border surveillance and data sharing, adequately trained and protected healthcare workers, predefined isolation and referral pathways, and community engagement structures led by trusted local stakeholders. Clinical research platforms with pre-approved protocols are also needed so that vaccine, therapeutic, and prophylactic candidates can be evaluated without avoidable delays during an active outbreak[26, 29]. Rationale and Scope of the Review This review provides a comprehensive evaluation of the terminology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment, vaccination, and IPC strategies related to Ebola, drawing on evidence from previous outbreaks and current international guidance. Particular emphasis is placed on the evolving 2026 BDBV outbreak, its epidemiological and public health implications, and persistent species-specific gaps in prevention and treatment. In contrast to previous reviews, which have focused predominantly on EBOV, this review integrates the evolving epidemiology of the 2026 BDBV outbreak with species-specific evidence on diagnosis, prevention, investigational therapeutics, One Health-based surveillance, and practical clinical management. Review Methodology Search Strategy A targeted literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus from database inception through July 2026. The search strategy combined the terms “Ebola disease,” “Ebola virus disease,” “Bundibugyo virus,” “BDBV,” “Sudan virus,” “SUDV,” “Orthoebolavirus,” and “filovirus” with terms related to epidemiology, outbreaks, pathogenesis, transmission, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, case definitions, treatment, therapeutics, vaccination, IPC, contact tracing, and long-term sequelae. Boolean operators were used, and the reference lists of relevant reviews, guidelines, and key original studies were screened to identify additional publications. Official guidelines, case definitions, surveillance updates, outbreak reports, and media briefings issued by the WHO and its regional offices, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), European CDC (ECDC), UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses, Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Health, and other relevant public health and regulatory authorities were also reviewed. Selected conference abstracts and proceedings were considered only when they provided relevant historical or time-sensitive information unavailable in full peer-reviewed publications and contained sufficient methodological or outcome detail. Eligibility Criteria Peer-reviewed original studies, clinical trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, authoritative guidelines, and official institutional reports relevant to human Orthoebolavirus infections were considered. Recent evidence and current international recommendations were prioritized, whereas seminal historical publications were retained when necessary. Preclinical and animal studies were included only when they provided relevant evidence on pathogenesis, vaccine candidates, or investigational therapeutic approaches for which human data were limited. The peer-reviewed literature search was restricted to articles published in English, although relevant national guidance published in Turkish was also considered. Duplicate records, dissertations, non-peer-reviewed commentaries, publications outside the clinical, epidemiological, diagnostic, preventive, or therapeutic scope of the review, and documents lacking sufficient relevant information were excluded. Study Selection and Data Synthesis Retrieved records were independently screened at the title and abstract levels by two authors, and the full texts of potentially relevant publications were independently assessed. Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus. Given the narrative nature of this review, the evidence was synthesized qualitatively and organized into thematic sections. Particular attention was given to distinguishing EBOV-specific human evidence from findings related to other Orthoebolavirus species and from preclinical or animal data. No formal protocol registration, standardized risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative evidence synthesis was performed. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Ebola disease (EBOD) is a severe viral illness with a high mortality rate caused by viruses of the genus Orthoebolavirus within the family Filoviridae. The emergence of a new outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in Ituri Province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo on May 15, 2026, along with the detection of cross-border cases in Uganda, has once again underscored the global public health significance of EBOD. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current terminology and classification, pathogenesis, modes of transmission, clinical and laboratory findings, diagnostic methods, case definitions, treatment approaches, Infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, contact tracing, vaccination strategies, and long-term sequelae associated with EBOD. Currently licensed vaccines and monoclonal antibody therapies are approved only for Orthoebolavirus zairense, limiting treatment options during BDBV outbreaks. Accelerating the development of pan-filovirus vaccines and therapeutics, strengthening early diagnostic capacity, and improving IPC infrastructure remain key priorities. Introduction Definition, Classification, and Current Terminology Ebola disease (EBOD) is a severe viral illness caused by viruses of the genus Orthoebolavirus within the family Filoviridae. Under the current classification, the principal Orthoebolavirus species known to cause human disease include Ebola virus (Orthoebolavirus zairense, EBOV), Sudan virus (Orthoebolavirus sudanense, SUDV), Bundibugyo virus (Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense, BDBV), and Taï Forest virus (Orthoebolavirus taiense, TAFV). The diseases caused by these viruses are designated Ebola virus disease (EVD), Sudan virus disease (SVD), Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), and Taï Forest virus disease, respectively. Thus, the term “Ebola disease” is used as a broad designation for diseases caused by different Orthoebolavirus species[1, 2]. History and Epidemiology EBOD was first recognized in 1976 during simultaneous outbreaks in present-day South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), caused by SUDV and EBOV, respectively. Subsequent outbreaks occurred predominantly in Central and East Africa, particularly in the DRC, Uganda, Gabon, and Sudan. Although the magnitude and mortality of outbreaks have varied according to viral species and epidemiological context, EBOV outbreaks have generally been associated with higher case-fatality rates. The 2014-2016 West African outbreak, initially reported in Guinea and subsequently spreading to Liberia and Sierra Leone, remains the largest EVD outbreak recorded to date, with more than 28,000 cases and 11,308 deaths. Limited healthcare capacity, inadequate surveillance systems, deficiencies in infection prevention and control (IPC), urban transmission, and extensive population mobility contributed to its rapid expansion. Travel-associated cases identified in Africa, Europe, and North America further underscored the potential for international dissemination of the disease. Recurrent outbreaks have continued, particularly in the DRC, including the 2018-2020 outbreak, which resulted in 3,470 cases and 2,287 deaths. The 2022 outbreak in Uganda further underscored the persistent public health significance of SUDV[3-5]. Mortality varies according to the causative viral species, access to healthcare, and the epidemiological and clinical characteristics of individual outbreaks. Comparative epidemiological characteristics, pooled case-fatality rates, and currently available vaccines and therapeutic options for EBOV, SUDV, and BDBV are summarized in Table 1. Overall mortality was 61.3% among patients treated in sub-Saharan Africa, compared with 24.5% among those treated outside sub-Saharan Africa[6]. Epidemiological risk is also shaped by the social context in which exposure occurs. Differences in exposure risk by sex and age appear to reflect social roles and caregiving responsibilities rather than established biological differences in susceptibility[20]. Environmental Drivers and One Health Perspective Environmental and social changes may influence both the risk of zoonotic spillover and the subsequent geographic spread of EBOD outbreaks. Changes in land use, including deforestation and other forms of forest conversion, may modify human-wildlife interfaces and increase opportunities for contact with potential animal reservoirs. A spatial analysis of 27 Ebola outbreak sites and 280 control locations in Central and West Africa found that outbreak occurrence near the margins of the rainforest biome was associated with dense forest loss during the preceding 2 years. However, this observational association does not demonstrate that forest loss alone causes EBOD outbreaks, and the mechanisms connecting environmental change, human-wildlife contact, and zoonotic spillover remain incompletely understood[21]. Following a spillover event, transport connectivity and population mobility may facilitate geographic dissemination by connecting remote outbreak locations with other settlements and population centers. An analysis of EBOV outbreaks found that the extent of road and river networks surrounding spillover sites was significantly associated with the number of cases recorded during the first 100 days of an outbreak[22]. The 2014-2016 West African epidemic further demonstrated how introduction into capital cities, extensive population mobility, and cross-border movement, coupled with weak surveillance, inadequate IPC, and strained healthcare systems, can facilitate sustained transmission and international spread[3-5]. However, the infrastructure analysis did not incorporate indicators of population density, settlement size, or urban-rural status and therefore did not directly assess urbanization as an independent determinant of outbreak spread[22]. Moreover, because the analysis included only EBOV outbreaks, these findings should be extrapolated cautiously to outbreaks caused by other Orthoebolavirus species. Taken together, these findings support a One Health approach that integrates human disease surveillance with animal and environmental monitoring while fostering coordination among public health, veterinary, wildlife, and environmental authorities. Incorporating land-use and population-connectivity data into this multisectoral framework may improve assessment of spillover risk, facilitate early outbreak detection, and strengthen preparedness. Nevertheless, evidence linking specific environmental and social drivers to Ebola emergence remains predominantly observational, and causal relationships have not been definitively established[23]. The 2026 BVD Outbreak: Epidemiological Characteristics, Public Health Response, and Lessons Learned On May 15, 2026, an outbreak of BVD was declared in Ituri Province in northeastern DRC, and outbreak-associated cases were subsequently identified in Uganda. As of July 21, 2026, the DRC had reported 2,536 laboratory-confirmed cases and 1,033 deaths among confirmed cases across Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, and Tshopo provinces. Uganda had reported 20 confirmed cases, including 2 deaths, and 1 probable case resulting in death. Fifteen confirmed infections were imported from the DRC, whereas 5 resulted from secondary transmission among contacts and healthcare workers. No sustained community transmission had been documented, and the most recent confirmed case in Uganda was identified on June 21, 2026. An imported case was also reported in France; the patient subsequently recovered, and no secondary transmission was detected. Because case investigations, laboratory confirmation, and data harmonization were ongoing, these reported figures should be considered provisional[24-27]. Reported cases accumulated considerably faster than during previous major EBOD outbreaks. analysis.summary_en: This review provides an updated overview of Ebola disease (EBOD), focusing on the 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and cross-border cases in Uganda. It outlines the current terminology and classification of EBOD, emphasizing that the term 'Ebola disease' is used as a broad designation for diseases caused by different Orthoebolavirus species. The review highlights that the largest recorded outbreak was the 2014-2016 West African outbreak, which had over 28,000 cases and 11,308 deaths. It also notes that currently licensed vaccines and monoclonal antibody therapies are only approved for Orthoebolavirus zairense, limiting treatment options during BDBV outbreaks. The review underscores the need for accelerating the development of pan-filovirus vaccines and therapeutics, strengthening early diagnostic capacity, and improving infection prevention and control (IPC) infrastructure to address the global public health significance of EBOD.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 埃博拉病 (EBOD) 是一种严重的病毒性疾病,由丝状病毒科正埃博拉病毒属病毒引起,发病率很高。该综述重点关注当前的术语和分类、发病机制、传播 模式、临床和实验室检查结果、诊断方法、病例定义、治疗 方法、感染预防和控制 (IPC) 措施、接触者追踪、疫苗接种 策略以及与 EBOD 相关的长期后遗症。核心问题是在 2026 本迪布焦病毒 暴发 的背景下评估 EBOD 的流行病学、临床和治疗方面。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述基于对文献的综合分析,包括刚果民主共和国的2026年本迪布焦病毒暴发和乌干达的跨境病例。证据包括 暴发 的历史数据、临床发现和公共卫生影响。该评论没有明确报告荟萃分析或共识过程,但它提供了当前对 EBOD 理解的详细概述。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 2014-2016 年西非 暴发 最初在几内亚报告,随后传播到利比里亚和塞拉利昂,仍然是迄今为止记录的最大埃博拉病毒病 暴发,病例数超过 28,000 例,死亡人数 11,308 人。由不同正埃博拉病毒属引起的疾病分别被指定为埃博拉病毒病 (EVD)、苏丹病毒病(SVD)、本迪布焦病毒病(BVD)和塔伊森林病毒病。“埃博拉病”一词是对由不同正埃博拉病毒属引起的疾病的广义称呼。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该审查强调,目前获得许可的 疫苗 和单克隆抗体疗法仅批准用于扎伊尔正博拉病毒,限制了 BDBV 暴发 期间 治疗 的选择。死亡率 根据致病病毒种类、获得医疗保健的机会以及个体 暴发 的流行病学和临床特征而有所不同。审查还指出,在非洲、欧洲和北美发现的与旅行相关的病例进一步凸显了该疾病国际传播的可能性。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 加快泛丝状病毒 疫苗 和治疗方法的开发、加强早期诊断能力以及改善感染预防和控制 (IPC) 基础设施仍然是关键优先事项。2026年5月15日,刚果民主共和国伊图里省出现由本迪布焦病毒(BDBV)引起的新暴发,加上乌干达发现跨境病例,再次凸显了EBOD对全球公共卫生的重要性。有限的医疗保健能力、不足的监测系统、感染预防和控制(IPC)的缺陷、城市传播以及广泛的人口流动导致了2014-2016年西非暴发的快速扩张。

analysis_zh.scope_and_question: 埃博拉病 (EBOD) 是一种严重的病毒性疾病,由丝状病毒科正埃博拉病毒属病毒引起,发病率很高。该综述重点关注当前的术语和分类、发病机制、传播 模式、临床和实验室检查结果、诊断方法、病例定义、治疗 方法、感染预防和控制 (IPC) 措施、接触者追踪、疫苗接种 策略以及与 EBOD 相关的长期后遗症。核心问题是在 2026 本迪布焦病毒 暴发 的背景下评估 EBOD 的流行病学、临床和治疗方面。
analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述基于对文献的综合分析,包括刚果民主共和国的2026年本迪布焦病毒暴发和乌干达的跨境病例。证据包括 暴发 的历史数据、临床发现和公共卫生影响。该评论没有明确报告荟萃分析或共识过程,但它提供了当前对 EBOD 理解的详细概述。
analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 2014-2016 年西非 暴发 最初在几内亚报告,随后传播到利比里亚和塞拉利昂,仍然是迄今为止记录的最大埃博拉病毒病 暴发,病例数超过 28,000 例,死亡人数 11,308 人。由不同正埃博拉病毒属引起的疾病分别被指定为埃博拉病毒病 (EVD)、苏丹病毒病(SVD)、本迪布焦病毒病(BVD)和塔伊森林病毒病。“埃博拉病”一词是对由不同正埃博拉病毒属引起的疾病的广义称呼。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该审查强调,目前获得许可的 疫苗 和单克隆抗体疗法仅批准用于扎伊尔正博拉病毒,限制了 BDBV 暴发 期间 治疗 的选择。死亡率 根据致病病毒种类、获得医疗保健的机会以及个体 暴发 的流行病学和临床特征而有所不同。审查还指出,在非洲、欧洲和北美发现的与旅行相关的病例进一步凸显了该疾病国际传播的可能性。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 加快泛丝状病毒 疫苗 和治疗方法的开发、加强早期诊断能力以及改善感染预防和控制 (IPC) 基础设施仍然是关键优先事项。2026年5月15日,刚果民主共和国伊图里省出现由本迪布焦病毒(BDBV)引起的新暴发,加上乌干达发现跨境病例,再次凸显了EBOD对全球公共卫生的重要性。有限的医疗保健能力、不足的监测系统、感染预防和控制(IPC)的缺陷、城市传播以及广泛的人口流动导致了2014-2016年西非暴发的快速扩张。

papers.title: NEXTEBOVAX: ONTCIJFERING VAN ORTHOEBOLAVIRUS-IMMUNITEIT Mechanismen van homologe en heterologe bescherming tegen orthoebolavirussen in preklinische modellen
papers.abstract: The family Filoviridae consists of antigenically distinct human pathogenic viruses such as, among others, Ebola virus, Marburg virus and Sudan virus. Filoviruses have evolved sophisticated ways of evading the immune response thereby causing high mortality rates, and outbreaks are recurring over the past decades. Only two vaccines have been granted market authorization by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for Ebola virus, yet none for the other highly pathogenic filoviruses. The aim of this PhD thesis is to study the protective efficacy of transgenic yellow fever 17D vectored vaccine candidates targeting the glycoprotein of the distinct filoviruses in small animal models, and with sera derived from small animal models. To that end, we will make use of pseudotyped filoviruses, such as recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses carrying the glycoprotein of these filoviruses, which can be used within biosafety level 2 facilities, as well as a wide range of assays to evaluate the immune response elicited by the experimental vaccine candidates to ultimately determine the quality of the protective efficacy of these vaccine candidates.​

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the protective efficacy of transgenic yellow fever 17D vectored vaccine candidates against distinct filoviruses, given the high mortality rates and recurring outbreaks caused by these viruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The research focused on small animal models and utilized sera derived from these models to evaluate vaccine candidates targeting the glycoprotein of various filoviruses, including Ebola virus and its related species.
analysis.methods: The study employed pseudotyped filoviruses, such as recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses carrying the glycoprotein of these filoviruses, and conducted a wide range of assays to assess the immune response elicited by the experimental vaccine candidates.
analysis.main_results: The protective efficacy of the vaccine candidates was evaluated using pseudotyped filoviruses and sera from small animal models, with the goal of determining their effectiveness against the targeted filoviruses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the vaccine candidates may offer protection against the targeted filoviruses, contributing to the understanding of immune mechanisms against these pathogens.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results may inform the development of more effective vaccines for filoviruses, particularly in preclinical settings, and support future research into broader immune protection strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to preclinical models and does not provide direct evidence on human efficacy, which may affect the generalisability of the findings. The evidence strength is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This PhD thesis investigates the protective efficacy of transgenic yellow fever 17D vectored vaccine candidates targeting the glycoprotein of distinct filoviruses in small animal models. The study highlights the challenges posed by filoviruses, which have evolved mechanisms to evade the immune system, leading to high mortality rates and recurring outbreaks. The research employs pseudotyped filoviruses and a range of assays to evaluate immune responses, aiming to improve vaccine development for these viruses. The findings suggest potential protective mechanisms, which could inform future vaccine strategies. However, the study is limited to preclinical models, and its evidence strength is moderate due to the lack of direct human data.

papers.abstract_zh: 丝状病毒科由抗原性不同的人类致病病毒组成,例如 埃博拉病毒、马尔堡病毒和苏丹病毒。丝状病毒已经进化出复杂的方法来逃避 免疫应答,从而导致高 死亡率 率,并且 暴发 在过去几十年中不断出现。只有两种 疫苗 已获得欧洲药品管理局 (EMA) 的 埃博拉病毒 市场授权,但其他高致病性丝状病毒尚未获得市场授权。本博士论文的目的是研究转基因黄热病 17D 载体 疫苗 候选药物在小动物模型和小动物模型血清中的保护功效,该候选药物针对不同丝状病毒的糖蛋白。为此,我们将利用假型丝状病毒,例如携带这些丝状病毒糖蛋白的重组水泡性口炎病毒,可在生物安全2级设施中使用,以及评估实验性疫苗候选物引起的免疫应答的广泛测定,以最终确定这些疫苗候选物的保护功效的质量。

papers.title: Model-guided placement of decentralized diagnostics for spatial control of the 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola epidemic
papers.abstract: Before 2026, Bundibugyo virus disease had only two recognized outbreaks. By August 2026, delayed recognition and multi-day sample transport in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo had contributed to a large, spatially dispersed epidemic. We hypothesized that model-guided placement of decentralized diagnostics in frontier health zones could help contain spatial spread by acting as a spatial fence: delayed recognition would be converted into timely polymerase chain reaction (PCR) confirmation, isolation, and contact tracing before imported lineages became established. We fit a Bayesian spatial branching process to public situation reports through 2 August 2026, with Flowminder movement and a latent-burden anchor. Lineages had overdispersed offspring, PCR access and turnaround, clinical recognition, isolation, tracing, safe burial, and local behaviour change. Because the observed history did not identify future control, we assumed a national response ramp yielding West-Africa-scale status-quo burden and replayed 2,000 posterior trees with 5-100 zone-level PCR laboratories, deployment delays of 0-180 days, and postmortem rapid diagnostic test (RDT) coverage. The posterior reproduced case, death, latent-burden, and spatial targets. Speed dominated: 35 PCR laboratories averted a median 49% of future deaths if deployed immediately, 38% after 14 days, and 11% after 60 days, with 90% prediction intervals of 30-65%, 23-53%, and 5-20%, respectively. Placement also mattered: with a 30-day delay, model-informed placement averted 18-33% of future deaths with 20-100 laboratories, versus 1-8% under random placement. Postmortem RDTs partly filled gaps left by live-case detection, increasing future deaths averted from 26% to 41% with 20 laboratories, a 14-day delay, and 75% coverage. Decentralized diagnostics can slow spatial spread when they are placed ahead of likely importations and paired with staffing, isolation, tracing, and safe-burial capacity.

papers.title_zh: 模型引导的分散诊断放置,用于 2026 年本迪布焦埃博拉疫情的空间控制
papers.source_body_en: Before 2026, Bundibugyo virus disease had only two recognized outbreaks. By August 2026, delayed recognition and multi-day sample transport in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo had contributed to a large, spatially dispersed epidemic. We hypothesized that model-guided placement of decentralized diagnostics in frontier health zones could help contain spatial spread by acting as a spatial fence: delayed recognition would be converted into timely polymerase chain reaction (PCR) confirmation, isolation, and contact tracing before imported lineages became established. We fit a Bayesian spatial branching process to public situation reports through 2 August 2026, with Flowminder movement and a latent-burden anchor. Lineages had overdispersed offspring, PCR access and turnaround, clinical recognition, isolation, tracing, safe burial, and local behaviour change. Because the observed history did not identify future control, we assumed a national response ramp yielding West-Africa-scale status-quo burden and replayed 2,000 posterior trees with 5-100 zone-level PCR laboratories, deployment delays of 0-180 days, and postmortem rapid diagnostic test (RDT) coverage. The posterior reproduced case, death, latent-burden, and spatial targets. Speed dominated: 35 PCR laboratories averted a median 49% of future deaths if deployed immediately, 38% after 14 days, and 11% after 60 days, with 90% prediction intervals of 30-65%, 23-53%, and 5-20%, respectively. Placement also mattered: with a 30-day delay, model-informed placement averted 18-33% of future deaths with 20-100 laboratories, versus 1-8% under random placement. Postmortem RDTs partly filled gaps left by live-case detection, increasing future deaths averted from 26% to 41% with 20 laboratories, a 14-day delay, and 75% coverage. Decentralized diagnostics can slow spatial spread when they are placed ahead of likely importations and paired with staffing, isolation, tracing, and safe-burial capacity.
papers.abstract_zh: 2026 年之前,本迪布焦病毒病只有两个公认的 暴发。到 2026 年 8 月,刚果民主共和国东部的延迟识别和多天的样本运输导致了大规模、空间分散的流行病。我们假设,在边境卫生区以模型为指导放置分散诊断可以通过充当空间围栏来帮助遏制空间传播:在输入谱系建立之前,延迟识别将转化为及时的聚合酶链反应(PCR)确认、隔离和接触者追踪。我们将贝叶斯空间分支过程与截至 2026 年 8 月 2 日的公共状况报告相匹配,其中包括 Flowminder 运动和潜在负担锚。谱系有过度分散的后代、PCR 获取和周转、临床识别、隔离、追踪、安全埋葬和当地行为改变。由于观察到的历史并不能确定未来的控制,我们假设国家响应斜坡产生西非规模的现状负担,并通过 5-100 个区域级 PCR 实验室重播了 2,000 棵后树,部署延迟为 0-180 天,并进行了事后快速诊断测试 (RDT) 覆盖。后面再现的病例、死亡、潜在负担和空间目标。速度占主导地位:如果立即部署,35 个 PCR 实验室可避免未来死亡的中位数为 49%,14 天后可避免 38%,60 天后可避免 11%,90% 预测区间分别为 30-65%、23-53% 和 5-20%。安置也很重要:延迟 30 天后,在 20-100 个实验室中,基于模型的安置可以避免 18-33% 的未来死亡,而随机安置则为 1-8%。尸检 RDT 部分填补了活体病例检测留下的空白,通过 20 个实验室、14 天的延迟和 75% 的覆盖率,将未来的死亡人数从 26% 提高到 41%。当分散的诊断先于可能的输入并与人员配备、隔离、追踪和安全埋葬能力相结合时,可以减缓空间传播。

papers.title: Intracellular pathogen manipulation of ER-phagy: direct receptor targeting and indirect pathway perturbation.
papers.abstract: Selective autophagy of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER-phagy) maintains intracellular homeostasis by selectively removing damaged ER membranes and contained misfolded proteins. This review delineates the core molecular mechanisms of canonical autophagy, then systematically describes three types of ER-phagy (macro-ER-phagy, micro-ER-phagy, and vesicular ER-phagy), their signature receptors, subdomain specificities, and regulatory mechanisms, alongside a comparative analysis of the evolutionary divergence between yeast and mammalian ER-phagy receptor systems. At the direct regulation level, diverse intracellular pathogen strategies targeting ER-phagy receptors are examined, including proteasomal degradation and spatial sequestration of FAM134B by viruses, non-canonical micro-ER-phagy hijacking by retroviruses, constitutive antiviral defense mediated by FAM134B against Ebola virus, and bidirectional modulation of this receptor by bacterial effectors and pathogen-associated molecular patterns. At the indirect regulation level, intracellular pathogen-mediated perturbation of upstream nodes-including the UPR, ERAD, ER-RQC/UFMylation, and core macroautophagy machinery-is summarized. These findings underscore the dual role of ER-phagy as both a host defense barrier and a target for pathogen exploitation, providing novel insights into intracellular pathogenic mechanism.

papers.source_body_en: Selective autophagy of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER-phagy) maintains intracellular homeostasis by selectively removing damaged ER membranes and contained misfolded proteins. This review delineates the core molecular mechanisms of canonical autophagy, then systematically describes three types of ER-phagy (macro-ER-phagy, micro-ER-phagy, and vesicular ER-phagy), their signature receptors, subdomain specificities, and regulatory mechanisms, alongside a comparative analysis of the evolutionary divergence between yeast and mammalian ER-phagy receptor systems. At the indirect regulation level, intracellular pathogen-mediated perturbation of upstream nodes-including the UPR, ERAD, ER-RQC/UFMylation, and core macroautophagy machinery-is summarized. These findings underscore the dual role of ER-phagy as both a host defense barrier and a target for pathogen exploitation, providing novel insights into intracellular pathogenic mechanism.

papers.title: The vaccination paradox: how East Africa’s success in Ebola vaccine preparedness may be creating new public expectations for future outbreaks
papers.abstract: This perspective synthesizes published evidence on Ebola vaccination and outbreak preparedness in Africa. Successful vaccination against Zaire ebolavirus has strengthened vaccine-based outbreak control but may also create a preparedness risk when public expectations exceed species-specific vaccine availability. We propose the Vaccine Expectation Gap, Vaccine Anticipation and Species-Specific Vaccine Literacy as linked, hypothesis-generating constructs, supported by a Preparedness Trust Contract for practical implementation. The framework draws on expectation-disconfirmation and crisis and emergency risk communication theories and distinguishes established evidence from interpretation and testable hypotheses. Recent Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus outbreaks illustrate the relevance of this gap because licensed vaccines remain species-specific. Evidence is concentrated in Uganda, making broader East African application a hypothesis requiring empirical testing. If validated, the framework could strengthen risk communication, community trust and regional health-security planning.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review explores how East Africa's success in Ebola vaccine preparedness, particularly against Zaire ebolavirus, may influence public expectations during future outbreaks. It focuses on the implications of vaccine availability and preparedness for managing Ebola virus disease and related outbreaks.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review synthesizes published evidence on Ebola vaccination and outbreak preparedness in Africa. It draws on theories of expectation-disconfirmation and crisis communication, distinguishing between established evidence and interpretations.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review highlights the potential for a 'Vaccine Expectation Gap' when public expectations exceed the availability of species-specific vaccines. It proposes constructs like 'Vaccine Anticipation' and 'Species-Specific Vaccine Literacy' as tools for improving preparedness and trust.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The evidence is concentrated in Uganda, limiting the generalizability of findings to broader East Africa. The framework is presented as hypothesis-generating, requiring empirical validation to strengthen its application in public health and risk communication.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that the framework could enhance risk communication, community trust, and regional health-security planning if validated. It emphasizes the need for empirical testing and practical implementation of the constructs proposed.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines how East Africa's success in Ebola vaccine preparedness, particularly against Zaire ebolavirus, may shape public expectations during future outbreaks. It identifies the 'Vaccine Expectation Gap' as a critical issue when vaccine availability does not meet public anticipation. The review proposes constructs like 'Vaccine Anticipation' and 'Species-Specific Vaccine Literacy' to address this gap and improve outbreak preparedness. However, the evidence is primarily from Uganda, limiting broader applicability. The framework remains hypothesis-generating and requires empirical validation. If validated, it could enhance risk communication, community trust, and regional health-security planning, offering actionable insights for future outbreaks.

papers.title_zh: 疫苗接种 悖论:东非在埃博拉 疫苗 准备工作中取得的成功如何可能为未来创造新的公众期望 暴发
papers.source_body_en: This perspective synthesizes published evidence on Ebola vaccination and outbreak preparedness in Africa. Successful vaccination against Zaire ebolavirus has strengthened vaccine-based outbreak control but may also create a preparedness risk when public expectations exceed species-specific vaccine availability. We propose the Vaccine Expectation Gap, Vaccine Anticipation and Species-Specific Vaccine Literacy as linked, hypothesis-generating constructs, supported by a Preparedness Trust Contract for practical implementation. The framework draws on expectation-disconfirmation and crisis and emergency risk communication theories and distinguishes established evidence from interpretation and testable hypotheses. Recent Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus outbreaks illustrate the relevance of this gap because licensed vaccines remain species-specific. Evidence is concentrated in Uganda, making broader East African application a hypothesis requiring empirical testing. If validated, the framework could strengthen risk communication, community trust and regional health-security planning.
papers.abstract_zh: 这一观点综合了已发表的有关非洲埃博拉病毒 疫苗接种 和 暴发 防范的证据。疫苗接种 成功对抗扎伊尔埃博拉病毒加强了基于 疫苗 的 暴发 控制,但当公众期望超过特定物种 疫苗 的可用性时,也可能会产生准备风险。我们提出 疫苗 期望差距、疫苗 预期和特定物种 疫苗 素养作为相互关联的假设生成结构,并由准备信托合同支持以进行实际实施。该框架借鉴了预期否定以及危机和紧急情况风险沟通理论,并将既定证据与解释和可检验的假设区分开来。最近的苏丹病毒和本迪布焦病毒 暴发 说明了这一差距的相关性,因为获得许可的 疫苗 仍然具有物种特异性。证据集中在乌干达,这使得更广泛的东非应用成为需要实证检验的假设。如果得到验证,该框架可以加强风险沟通、社区信任和区域卫生安全规划。

papers.title: Fear of Ebola and willingness to work during an Ebola outbreak among healthcare workers in a non-affected city of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction : The ongoing Ebola outbreak in the DRC highlights the urgent need to assess healthcare workers’ readiness to respond, as they constitute a particularly exposed population during Ebola virus disease outbreaks. This study aimed to assess the level of fear of Ebola and to analyse its association with willingness to work in the event of a potential outbreak in Lubumbashi, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Methods A descriptive cross-sectional observational study with an analytical component was conducted from 24 May to 22 June 2026 among healthcare workers practising in the city of Lubumbashi, a city not directly affected by the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the DRC. Convenience sampling was used to include 135 participants. Fear of Ebola and willingness to work were assessed using two 10-item scales, with satisfactory internal consistency (Cronbach’s α: 0.75 and 0.86, respectively). Associations were assessed using bivariate analyses and multivariable logistic regression. Results The median age of participants was 30 years and the median professional experience was 4 years; 63.7% were men and 67.4% were physicians. Fear was particularly related to concerns about the safety of relatives (40.3/50) and the risk of transmitting Ebola to family members (39.0/50). papers.title: The geography of waiting: surveillance latency as the hidden driver of Ebola risk in East Africa
papers.abstract: Ebola virus disease remains a persistent public health threat in East Africa, yet preparedness strategies continue to emphasise response after outbreaks are recognised rather than the period preceding detection. This Perspective argues that surveillance latency the cumulative delay between the earliest clinically meaningful signal and organised public health action is a critical but insufficiently measured determinant of Ebola risk. Although diagnostic and reporting delays have been widely documented, they are often treated as isolated operational challenges. We introduce the concept of the geography of waiting, an integrative framework that links biological, clinical, diagnostic, administrative and community delays to spatial inequalities in physical, technical and relational infrastructure. Unequal access to diagnostics, transportation, laboratory networks, trusted communication channels and community reporting systems creates substantial variation in detection timelines across settings. Where surveillance latency is prolonged, transmission may continue undetected, increasing the likelihood of larger and more complex outbreaks. Drawing on evidence from outbreaks in Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Guinea and Rwanda, we examine the mechanisms underlying delayed detection and consider them alongside performance frameworks such as Uganda’s 7-1-7 strategy. We propose a practical approach that integrates syndromic and event-based surveillance, decentralised molecular testing, community early-warning systems and regional data sharing. Because shorter detection intervals are associated with smaller eventual outbreaks in the cases reviewed here, reducing surveillance latency is a plausible high-value investment for Ebola preparedness, although this remains a hypothesis pending formal economic evaluation rather than an established finding.

papers.title_original: The geography of waiting: surveillance latency as the hidden driver of Ebola risk in East Africa

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on Ebola viruses and their associated disease, examining how surveillance latency contributes to the risk of outbreaks in East Africa. The central question is whether addressing surveillance latency can improve preparedness and reduce outbreak size.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a Perspective article that does not conduct a systematic or meta-analytic review. It draws on evidence from outbreaks in Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Guinea, and Rwanda, and considers performance frameworks like Uganda’s 7-1-7 strategy. The review does not report on study counts, databases, or formal eligibility criteria.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that surveillance latency, defined as the cumulative delay between the earliest clinically meaningful signal and public health action, is a critical but insufficiently measured determinant of Ebola risk. It highlights that shorter detection intervals are associated with smaller eventual outbreaks, suggesting that reducing latency could be a high-value investment for preparedness.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that diagnostic and reporting delays are often treated as isolated operational challenges rather than part of a broader system of surveillance latency. It also identifies a gap in formal economic evaluation of reducing surveillance latency as a preparedness strategy.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review proposes integrating syndromic and event-based surveillance, decentralised molecular testing, community early-warning systems, and regional data sharing to reduce surveillance latency. It suggests that these measures could enhance outbreak detection and control, although this remains a hypothesis requiring further validation.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the role of surveillance latency in shaping Ebola risk in East Africa. It argues that delays in detection, stemming from biological, clinical, diagnostic, administrative, and community factors, significantly influence outbreak size and complexity. The authors highlight that current strategies often focus on post-outbreak response rather than addressing the pre-detection period. They propose an integrative framework to improve surveillance systems, emphasizing the need for shorter detection intervals to mitigate larger outbreaks. While the review identifies potential benefits of reducing latency, it notes that this remains a hypothesis requiring formal economic evaluation. The implications suggest a shift in preparedness efforts toward proactive surveillance and regional collaboration.

elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该评论是一篇观点文章,不进行系统或荟萃分析评论。它借鉴了乌干达、刚果民主共和国、几内亚和卢旺达的 暴发 的证据,并考虑了乌干达 7-1-7 战略等绩效框架。该审查不报告研究数量、数据库或正式的资格标准。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 审查得出的结论是,监测 潜伏期(定义为最早有临床意义的信号与公共卫生行动之间的累积延迟)是埃博拉风险的一个关键但未充分测量的决定因素。它强调,较短的检测间隔与较小的最终 暴发 相关,这表明减少延迟可能是一项高价值的准备投资。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 审查指出,诊断和报告延迟通常被视为孤立的操作挑战,而不是更广泛的 监测 延迟系统的一部分。它还确定了减少 监测 延迟作为准备策略的正式经济评估中的差距。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 该评论建议整合基于症状和事件的 监测、分散分子测试、社区预警系统和区域数据共享,以减少 监测 延迟。它表明这些措施可以增强 暴发 的检测和控制,尽管这仍然是一个需要进一步验证的假设。

We introduce the concept of the geography of waiting, an integrative framework that links biological, clinical, diagnostic, administrative and community delays to spatial inequalities in physical, technical and relational infrastructure. Unequal access to diagnostics, transportation, laboratory networks, trusted communication channels and community reporting systems creates substantial variation in detection timelines across settings. Where surveillance latency is prolonged, transmission may continue undetected, increasing the likelihood of larger and more complex outbreaks. Drawing on evidence from outbreaks in Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Guinea and Rwanda, we examine the mechanisms underlying delayed detection and consider them alongside performance frameworks such as Uganda’s 7-1-7 strategy. We propose a practical approach that integrates syndromic and event-based surveillance, decentralised molecular testing, community early-warning systems and regional data sharing. Because shorter detection intervals are associated with smaller eventual outbreaks in the cases reviewed here, reducing surveillance latency is a plausible high-value investment for Ebola preparedness, although this remains a hypothesis pending formal economic evaluation rather than an established finding.

papers.title: Serological and transcriptomic response of African fruit bats to immune challenge with recombinant vaccines expressing Ebola or Nipah virus antigens
papers.abstract: Abstract Bats are hosts to diverse zoonotic viruses which can cause high case fatality rates in humans. Since detecting viruses in bats is difficult, antibodies are often used for surveillance, though their significance remains unclear in the absence of in vivo immunological studies. To address this knowledge gap, we measured antibody production and gene expression in bats following injection with vaccines encoding either a Nipah virus G glycoprotein or an Ebola virus GP glycoprotein. We selected two African bat species with overlapping ranges, Eidolon helvum (confirmed reservoir of henipaviruses) and Epomophorus gambianus (putative reservoir of filoviruses). Using a Luminex-based multiplex microsphere immunoassay and a pseudotype virus neutralization assay, we observed an increase in antibodies against the Nipah glycoprotein in most bats that received the Nipah vaccine. In contrast, we could only detect anti-Ebola glycoprotein antibodies in one bat species, Ep. gambianus, in response to the Ebola vaccine. Transcriptomic analysis in Ei. helvum revealed that genes involved in ISGylation and T-cell differentiation pathways were differentially expressed in response to the Ebola, but not the Nipah, vaccine. These results demonstrate species-specific differences in responses to antigen exposure, offering insights into bat adaptive immune systems and providing calibration for serological data from wild bats.
