analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the knowledge gap regarding antibody production and gene expression in bats following exposure to vaccines encoding Ebola or Nipah virus antigens, as detecting viruses in bats is difficult and the significance of antibodies remains unclear without in vivo immunological studies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved measuring antibody production and gene expression in two African bat species, Eidolon helvum (confirmed reservoir of henipaviruses) and Epomophorus gambianus (putative reservoir of filoviruses), following injection with vaccines expressing either a Nipah virus G glycoprotein or an Ebola virus GP glycoprotein.
analysis.methods: Antibody production was assessed using a Luminex-based multiplex microsphere immunoassay and a pseudotype virus neutralization assay, while transcriptomic analysis was conducted to evaluate gene expression changes in response to the vaccines.
analysis.main_results: Most bats that received the Nipah vaccine showed an increase in antibodies against the Nipah glycoprotein, whereas only one bat species, Epomophorus gambianus, exhibited detectable anti-Ebola glycoprotein antibodies in response to the Ebola vaccine. Transcriptomic analysis in Eidolon helvum revealed differential expression of genes involved in ISGylation and T-cell differentiation pathways following the Ebola vaccine, but not the Nipah vaccine.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The results demonstrate species-specific differences in immune responses to antigen exposure, providing insights into the adaptive immune systems of bats and offering calibration for serological data from wild bat populations.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings offer valuable insights into bat immune responses to filovirus antigens, which can inform the interpretation of serological data from wild bats and contribute to understanding the transmission dynamics of Ebola viruses.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the serological and transcriptomic responses of two African bat species, Eidolon helvum and Epomophorus gambianus, to vaccines expressing Ebola or Nipah virus antigens. The research aimed to address the knowledge gap regarding antibody production and gene expression in bats, as detecting viruses in bats is challenging and the significance of antibodies remains unclear without in vivo studies. Using Luminex-based assays and transcriptomic analysis, the study observed increased anti-Nipah glycoprotein antibodies in most Eidolon helvum bats following the Nipah vaccine, while only one Epomophorus gambianus bat showed detectable anti-Ebola glycoprotein antibodies. Transcriptomic analysis in Eidolon helvum revealed differential expression of genes involved in ISGylation and T-cell differentiation pathways in response to the Ebola vaccine. These results highlight species-specific immune responses to filovirus antigens, offering insights into bat adaptive immunity and aiding in the calibration of serological data from wild bats. The study is based on abstract-only evidence and has moderate strength due to its limited scope and lack of detailed in vivo immunological data.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及测量两种非洲蝙蝠——Eidolon helvum(确认为亨尼帕病毒的 储存宿主)和 Epomophorus gambianus(假定为丝状病毒的 储存宿主)在注射表达尼帕病毒 G 糖蛋白或 埃博拉病毒 GP 糖蛋白的 疫苗 后的抗体产生和基因表达。
elements_zh.methods: 使用基于 Luminex 的多重微球免疫测定和假型病毒中和测定评估抗体产生,同时进行转录组分析以评估响应 疫苗 的基因表达变化。
elements_zh.main_results: 大多数接受 Nipah 疫苗 的蝙蝠表现出针对 Nipah 糖蛋白的抗体增加,而只有一种蝙蝠物种(Epomophorus gambianus)表现出可检测到的针对埃博拉 疫苗 的抗埃博拉糖蛋白抗体。Eidolon helvum 中的转录组分析揭示了埃博拉 疫苗 后参与 ISGylation 和 T 细胞分化途径的基因的差异表达,但尼帕 疫苗 则不然。

elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为蝙蝠 免疫应答 丝状病毒抗原提供了宝贵的见解,可以为野生蝙蝠血清学数据的解释提供信息,并有助于了解 埃博拉病毒 的 传播 动态。

papers.summary_zh: 摘要 蝙蝠是多种人畜共患病病毒的宿主,这些病毒可导致人类高病死率。由于在蝙蝠体内检测病毒很困难,因此经常使用抗体来检测 监测,但在缺乏体内免疫学研究的情况下,其意义仍不清楚。为了解决这一知识差距,我们测量了注射编码尼帕病毒 G 糖蛋白或 埃博拉病毒 GP 糖蛋白的 疫苗 后蝙蝠体内抗体的产生和基因表达。我们选择了分布范围重叠的两种非洲蝙蝠物种:Eidolon helvum(确认为亨尼帕病毒 储存宿主)和 Epomophorus gambianus(假定为丝状病毒 储存宿主)。使用基于 Luminex 的多重微球免疫测定和假型病毒中和测定,我们观察到大多数接受 Nipah 疫苗 的蝙蝠体内针对 Nipah 糖蛋白的抗体有所增加。相比之下,我们只能在一种蝙蝠(Ep.)中检测到抗埃博拉糖蛋白抗体。gambianus,针对埃博拉病毒 疫苗。Ei 中的转录组分析。helvum 揭示,参与 ISGylation 和 T 细胞分化途径的基因在对埃博拉病毒的反应中存在差异表达,但对尼帕病毒 疫苗 则没有差异表达。这些结果证明了对抗原暴露反应的物种特异性差异,提供了对蝙蝠适应性免疫系统的深入了解,并为野生蝙蝠的血清学数据提供了校准。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在解决暴露于编码埃博拉病毒或尼帕病毒抗原的 疫苗 后蝙蝠中抗体产生和基因表达的知识差距,因为在蝙蝠中检测病毒很困难,并且在没有体内免疫学研究的情况下抗体的意义仍不清楚。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及测量两种非洲蝙蝠——Eidolon helvum(确认为亨尼帕病毒的 储存宿主)和 Epomophorus gambianus(假定为丝状病毒的 储存宿主)在注射表达尼帕病毒 G 糖蛋白或 埃博拉病毒 GP 糖蛋白的 疫苗 后的抗体产生和基因表达。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用基于 Luminex 的多重微球免疫测定和假型病毒中和测定评估抗体产生,同时进行转录组分析以评估响应 疫苗 的基因表达变化。
analysis_zh.main_results: 大多数接受 Nipah 疫苗 的蝙蝠表现出针对 Nipah 糖蛋白的抗体增加,而只有一种蝙蝠物种(Epomophorus gambianus)表现出可检测到的针对埃博拉 疫苗 的抗埃博拉糖蛋白抗体。Eidolon helvum 中的转录组分析揭示了埃博拉 疫苗 后参与 ISGylation 和 T 细胞分化途径的基因的差异表达,但尼帕 疫苗 则不然。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 结果证明了 免疫应答 对抗原暴露的物种特异性差异,提供了对蝙蝠适应性免疫系统的深入了解,并为野生蝙蝠种群的血清学数据提供了校准。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为蝙蝠 免疫应答 丝状病毒抗原提供了宝贵的见解,可以为野生蝙蝠血清学数据的解释提供信息,并有助于了解 埃博拉病毒 的 传播 动态。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究仅限于抽象证据,并且结果基于少数蝙蝠物种和个体,这可能会影响普遍性。由于缺乏详细的体内免疫学研究,证据强度中等。

news.content: Skip to main content Help Log in ReliefWeb Search Content Search What are you looking for? Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo DRC - Concept of Operations - Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) Outbreak, October 2026 Format Situation Report Sources Logistics Cluster WFP Posted 5 Oct 2026 Originally published 5 Oct 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 525.67 KB) Context The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) officially declared an Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) outbreak on 15 May 2026, following laboratory confirmation of the Bundibugyo strain in Ituri Province. As of 26 September 2026, the Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak remains concentrated in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with sustained transmission across multiple provinces and 8,067 confirmed cases and 3,901 deaths reported. The outbreak has expanded to 63 affected health zones across seven provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Bas-Uélé, Tshopo, and Sud-Ubangi. Uganda was officially declared the end of outbreak in late August 2026 following completion of the 42-day surveillance period with no onward transmission detected. While regional preparedness measures remain in place, the outbreak continues to pose a significant public health risk in eastern DRC, particularly in Ituri, North Kivu, and Haut-Uélé, where active transmission persists. Insecurity, population movements, displacement, difficult terrain, and limited access to health services continue to complicate response efforts and increase the risk of further spread within affected communities. The World Health Organization (WHO) declared the Ebola outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) on 17 May 2026 due to the risk of international spread and the need for a coordinated international response. The outbreak poses a significant risk of further transmission both within the DRC and across neighbouring countries, particularly Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Central African Republic, and South Sudan. Population movements and regional connectivity may further facilitate the spread of the disease to other major urban centres, including Butembo and Kisangani. At present, no vaccine is available for the Bundibugyo strain. This marks the seventeenth Ebola outbreak recorded in the DRC. In response, the Minister of Health in DRC has called for the mobilisation of technical and financial partners to support the national response plan. Compounding the public health crisis, eastern DRC remains severely affected by ongoing insecurity, population displacement, limited infrastructure, and access constraints. Recent developments in North and South Kivu have resulted in new population movements, including both displacement and returns to areas where basic services and security conditions remain fragile. Elsewhere, including in Maniema and Tanganyika provinces, ongoing instability continues to heighten humanitarian needs and increase protection risks, particularly for women and children, including exposure to gender-based violence. news.content_zh: 在实验室确认伊图里省的 Bundibugyo 菌株后,刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 于 2026 年 5 月 15 日正式宣布 埃博拉病毒病 (EVD) 暴发。截至 2026 年 9 月 26 日,暴发 仍集中在刚果民主共和国东部,7 个省的 63 个受影响卫生区报告了 8,067 例确诊病例和 3,901 例死亡。暴发 已扩展到伊图里、北基伍、南基伍、上韦莱、下韦莱、乔波和南乌班吉等地区,并构成重大公共卫生风险,特别是在伊图里、北基伍和上韦莱。由于存在国际传播风险,世界卫生组织 (WHO) 于 2026 年 5 月 17 日宣布 暴发 为国际关注的突发公共卫生事件 (PHEIC)。刚果民主共和国卫生部长呼吁动员技术和金融合作伙伴支持国家应对计划。然而,持续的不安全局势、人口流动和获得医疗服务的机会有限,继续使应对工作变得复杂化,并增加了受影响社区内进一步传播的风险。暴发 仍然是该地区公共卫生面临的严峻挑战。

WHO supports control efforts Kenya confirms first imported Bundibugyo virus disease case; WHO supports control efforts 6 October 2026 | News Release | Reading time: 4 min Kenya confirms first imported Bundibugyo virus disease case; WHO supports control efforts Nairobi—Following the confirmation by Kenyan authorities of the country's first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), the World Health Organization (WHO) is working closely with the Government of Kenya to intensify key control measures to prevent further spread of the virus. The government is strengthening its response coordination and case investigation, while monitoring and listing contacts for enhanced disease surveillance. At the core of the response efforts are screening at high-risk points of entry, and clear risk communication, while engaging communities to help prevent infection. These measures are rapidly being deployed to ensure the identification of cases and help contain further transmission. The patient, a Kenyan citizen, fell ill in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where they had been living, and was treated at several health facilities there. The patient then travelled by road to Kampala, Uganda through Beni on 2 October 2026, and flew to Nairobi, arriving on 3 October 2026. On arrival, the patient was transported to a hospital in Nairobi and was quickly isolated. Samples tested positive for Bundibugyo virus at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute. Despite supportive care, the patient died on the night of 5 October 2026 and was buried on 6 October 2026 in line with the country’s Ebola safe and dignified burial protocol. The Government of Kenya notified WHO of the case in line with the International Health Regulations (2005) on 6 October 2026. Kenya is the fourth country to confirm BVD. The Democratic Republic of the Congo is responding to an ongoing BVD outbreak, while Uganda, where the Bundibugyo virus species was first detected in 2007, ended the latest outbreak in August 2026. Most cases in Uganda were imported from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the remaining few were locally acquired among contacts and health workers linked to imported cases. France reported a travel-related case of BVD in June 2026. Health authorities in Kenya have so far listed 28 contacts, including family members and health workers who cared for the patient. They are also tracing 23 passengers and four crew members from the same flight, with arrangements underway for appropriate follow-up and quarantine of people assessed to be at risk. "Health emergency preparedness gives us a head start. Kenya has put important outbreak control measures in place. The priority now is to move swiftly to detect any further cases before the virus has an opportunity to spread. We're supporting the ongoing efforts to strengthen the response, and with rapid and coordinated action, we can prevent the virus from gaining a foothold and stop a potential larger outbreak," said Dr Mohamed Janabi, WHO Regional Director for Africa. Kenya has been on high alert since May 2026, when outbreaks were declared in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. As of 6 October 2026, Kenya has screened over 652 000 travellers entering the country, tested 267 suspected samples and trained around 5000 health workers on Ebola prevention and management. WHO and partners have supported Kenya’s Ministry of Health and National Public Health Institute in these efforts. This includes Ebola simulation exercises and training a national pool of rapid response trainers, among them responders who served during the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak. Isolation units across 27 high-risk counties in Kenya have been identified and assessed, case managers trained, and Ebola surveillance tools have been updated so that suspected cases can be quickly identified, reported and investigated. Risk communication and community engagement activities have also been strengthened through public messaging, media and community engagement, call centre support, and monitoring and responding to rumours and misinformation. WHO has also delivered about 1000 Ebola tests and 1000 personal protective equipment kits to high-risk counties in Kenya. Kenya's Ebola preparedness score, which tracks progress on key readiness measures such as surveillance, laboratory testing, isolation and treatment facilities and trained response teams, rose from 66% in May to 82% in July 2026. WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda or Kenya based on the currently available information. WHO continues to closely monitor and, where necessary, verify travel and trade measures in relation to this event. WHO calls for continued support to the response in affected countries. Global solidarity, along with government-led responses with engaged communities, is the best route to ending the outbreak. Note to editors: Bundibugyo virus disease is a severe, often fatal illness. It spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated materials. There are currently no approved vaccines or specific treatments for Bundibugyo virus disease, but candidate products are being evaluated in clinical trials. news.title_zh: 肯尼亚确认首例输入性本迪布焦病毒病病例;世卫组织支持控制努力
news.source_body_en: Kenya confirmed its first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) on 6 October 2026, following the patient's illness in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and subsequent travel through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient, a Kenyan citizen, was treated in the DRC and later isolated in Nairobi after arriving on 3 October 2026. Despite supportive care, the patient died on 5 October 2026, and the burial followed Kenya’s safe and dignified protocol. The government has listed 28 contacts, including family members and health workers, and is tracing 23 passengers and four crew members from the same flight. WHO is supporting Kenya with testing, training, and risk communication to prevent further spread. Kenya has screened over 652,000 travelers and trained 5,000 health workers since May 2026. The country is on high alert, with isolation units established in 27 high-risk counties and updated surveillance tools. The response is ongoing, with efforts to detect and contain any further cases. The situation remains under investigation, and WHO advises against travel or trade restrictions based on current information.

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo + 9 more IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 20 (21 - 27 September 2026) Format Situation Report Source IOM Posted 2 Oct 2026 Originally published 2 Oct 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 2.15 MB) SITUATION OVERVIEW According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as of 27 September 2026, the country had reported 8,116 confirmed cases of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, including 3,924 deaths, resulting in a case fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. Since the beginning of the outbreak, 63 health zones across 7 provinces have reported at least 1 confirmed case. Transmission remains concentrated in Ituri and North Kivu Provinces, with Ituri accounting for 76.2 per cent of cumulative confirmed cases nationwide, underscoring its continued role as the epicentre of the outbreak. Although the daily number of new confirmed cases has declined from earlier peaks observed during the outbreak, transmission continues across multiple provinces, and the outbreak remains a significant public health threat. On 27 September, the Ministry of Health reported 49 new confirmed cases and 23 confirmed deaths, including 18 community deaths. Transmission remains concentrated in Ituri (27), North Kivu (18) and Haut-Uélé (4). The continued occurrence of community deaths and ongoing transmission across multiple provinces points to persistent challenges in early detection, referral, contact follow-up and timely access to care. As of 27 September, the national contact follow-up rate stood at 75.9 per cent, underscoring the need for sustained investment in disease surveillance, case investigation and response capacities. The outbreak continues to evolve within a complex humanitarian and mobility context. Population movements associated with trade, livelihoods, displacement, health-seeking behaviour and family ties continue within outbreak-affected areas and across international borders. Continued transmission in eastern DRC reinforces the importance of preparedness measures in neighbouring countries connected through established mobility corridors, including disease surveillance, population mobility monitoring, referral systems, infection, prevention and control (IPC) and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE). Preparedness activities across affected and at-risk countries continue to be informed by findings from population mobility mapping (PMM), flow monitoring, preparedness assessments and cross-border risk analyses. These approaches support evidencebased prioritization of preparedness investments, including disease surveillance, referral systems, RCCE and operational readiness measures at points of entry (PoEs), border communities, displacement settings and other high-risk locations. In line with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) system-wide scale-up activation for infectious disease events, IOM continues to support outbreak response activities across affected and at-risk countries. Response and readiness activities remain ongoing in DRC, Uganda, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, while preparedness efforts continue in Angola, the Central African Republic (CAR), Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, the United Republic of Tanzania and Zambia to strengthen disease surveillance, operational readiness, community engagement and cross-border coordination capacities. news.source_body_en: The IOM Situation Report No. 20, dated 21-27 September 2026, highlights a multi-country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). As of 27 September, the DRC reported 8,116 confirmed cases and 3,924 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. Transmission is concentrated in Ituri (76.2 per cent of cases), North Kivu, and Haut-Uélé Provinces, indicating persistent challenges in early detection and access to care. The report notes that while daily case numbers have declined, community deaths continue, underscoring the ongoing public health threat. Response activities are ongoing in DRC and neighboring countries, including Uganda, Burundi, Rwanda, and South Sudan, with preparedness efforts also in Angola, the Central African Republic, Ethiopia, Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, Tanzania, and Zambia. These efforts focus on disease surveillance, community engagement, and cross-border coordination to mitigate risks.

Transmission continues across multiple provinces, and community deaths persist, indicating ongoing public health risks.

Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Kenya confirms its first Ebola death as outbreak spreads 10 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Basillioh RukangaNairobi AFP via Getty Images There are currently no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola but some have been trialled Kenya has confirmed its first ever case of Ebola - a Kenyan citizen who has been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo for the past seven years. Health Minister Aden Duale said the patient, who fell ill a month ago, and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo, died days after arriving in the capital, Nairobi. Duale said the patient boarded a flight on Saturday and underwent normal public screening at the main airport in Nairobi before he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city. Kenya's health ministry says it has since stepped up surveillance at airports and border crossings. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease. Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died. However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August. Since then, all known cases of the highly infectious disease have been in DR Congo. The virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment. There are however four vaccines in development, with human trials for one of them launched in July. Duale confirmed that the Kenyan national had tested positive for the Bundibugyo species. According to the minister, the patient first travelled by road from DR Congo to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi. Duale said that after being taken to the Nairobi Hospital, the patient was transferred to an isolation facility that was built during the Covid-19 pandemic. It was there that the patient "developed fever, chills, intense fatigue and weakness, painful swallowing, muscle pain and bleeding under the skin". "Doctors suspected a viral haemorrhagic fever based on his symptoms and travel history and collected samples for testing. The sample tested positive for Ebola Bundibugyo virus," Duale said. The patient died at 23:30 (20:30 GMT) on Monday and he was buried on Tuesday in line with public health safety protocols. At least 28 contacts, including family members and healthcare workers, have been identified, while health authorities are tracing a further 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the same flight. A senior health ministry official said the patient might have passed screening at the airport because the medication he was taking masked his symptoms. Kenya introduced tighter checks at airports and border posts after the outbreak was declared in DR Congo but these have now been further intensified. The health minister urged Kenyans "not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease". He asked health workers to be "extra vigilant and maintain the highest infection prevention and control measures regardless of the condition being treated". EPA The Kenyan Red Cross Society oversaw the man's burial in Nairobi on Tuesday The WHO has recorded 4,114 deaths out of 8,544 cases in the current outbreak, making it the largest ever recorded in DR Congo, where Ebola was first discovered in 1976. Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) believes the current toll could be even higher because of gaps in surveillance and testing in the war-torn country. On Monday, MSF said the virus was spreading "like a megafire", with new hotspots emerging in North Kivu province, which borders Ituri where the virus began. Since early September this had "intensified dramatically" with the province now accounting for nearly 40% of all newly confirmed cases nationwide, MSF said. Eastern DR Congo has been riven by decades of conflict, with multiple rebel groups operating in the region amid ethnic tensions and fighting for political power and control of lucrative natural resources. The crisis has led to the death and displacement of millions of people, and hampered the country's ability to develop and maintain functional health care systems and infrastructure. Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Kenya confirms its first Ebola death as outbreak spreads 10 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Basillioh RukangaNairobi AFP via Getty Images There are currently no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola but some have been trialled Kenya has confirmed its first ever case of Ebola - a Kenyan citizen who has been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo for the past seven years. Health Minister Aden Duale said the patient, who fell ill a month ago, and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo, died days after arriving in the capital, Nairobi. Duale said the patient boarded a flight on Saturday and underwent normal public screening at the main airport in Nairobi before he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city. Kenya's health ministry says it has since stepped up surveillance at airports and border crossings. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease. Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died. However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August. Since then, all known cases of the highly infectious disease have been in DR Congo. The virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment. There are however four vaccines in development, with human trials for one of them launched in July. Duale confirmed that the Kenyan national had tested positive for the Bundibugyo species. According to the minister, the patient first travelled by road from DR Congo to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi. Duale said that after being taken to the Nairobi Hospital, the patient was transferred to an isolation facility that was built during the Covid-19 pandemic. It was there that the patient "developed fever, chills, intense fatigue and weakness, painful swallowing, muscle pain and bleeding under the skin". "Doctors suspected a viral haemorrhagic fever based on his symptoms and travel history and collected samples for testing. The sample tested positive for Ebola Bundibugyo virus," Duale said. The patient died at 23:30 (20:30 GMT) on Monday and he was buried on Tuesday in line with public health safety protocols. At least 28 contacts, including family members and healthcare workers, have been identified, while health authorities are tracing a further 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the same flight. A senior health ministry official said the patient might have passed screening at the airport because the medication he was taking masked his symptoms. Kenya introduced tighter checks at airports and border posts after the outbreak was declared in DR Congo but these have now been further intensified. The health minister urged Kenyans "not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease". He asked health workers to be "extra vigilant and maintain the highest infection prevention and control measures regardless of the condition being treated". EPA The Kenyan Red Cross Society oversaw the man's burial in Nairobi on Tuesday The WHO has recorded 4,114 deaths out of 8,544 cases in the current outbreak, making it the largest ever recorded in DR Congo, where Ebola was first discovered in 1976. Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) believes the current toll could be even higher because of gaps in surveillance and testing in the war-torn country. On Monday, MSF said the virus was spreading "like a megafire", with new hotspots emerging in North Kivu province, which borders Ituri where the virus began. Since early September this had "intensified dramatically" with the province now accounting for nearly 40% of all newly confirmed cases nationwide, MSF said. Eastern DR Congo has been riven by decades of conflict, with multiple rebel groups operating in the region amid ethnic tensions and fighting for political power and control of lucrative natural resources. The crisis has led to the death and displacement of millions of people, and hampered the country's ability to develop and maintain functional health care systems and infrastructure. news.content_zh: 肯尼亚于 2026 年 10 月 6 日报告了首例本迪布焦 (Bundibugyo) 物种 埃博拉病毒 病例。该患者是一名在刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 生活了七年的肯尼亚公民,一个月前患病,在抵达内罗毕之前在刚果民主共和国的医院接受治疗。他于 10 月 5 日去世,并根据公共卫生协议于 10 月 6 日下葬。卫生部长亚丁·杜阿莱(Aden Duale)证实了这一病例,并表示患者的病毒检测呈阳性。已确定至少 28 名接触者,并正在进一步追踪 23 名乘客和 4 名机组人员。刚果民主共和国 暴发 始于 1976 年,已造成 8,544 例病例中的 4,114 人死亡,成为该国有记录以来最大规模的疫情。本迪布焦病毒通过与体液接触传播,目前尚无批准的 疫苗 或 治疗,尽管有四种 疫苗 正在开发中。肯尼亚加强了机场和边境检查,卫生部敦促保持警惕,防止传播。世界卫生组织于 8 月宣布刚果民主共和国已消除该疾病,但 暴发 仍在继续,北基伍省出现了新的热点,目前该省报告了近 40% 的病例。

news.source_body_en: The news report highlights Kenya's first confirmed case of Ebola virus, raising concerns about the country's preparedness and potential trade barriers within the East African Community (EAC). The article emphasizes the critical need for swift action in the next 72 hours to prevent the spread of the virus. It also mentions the Africa CDC team's planned visit to Kenya to assess the situation and provide guidance. Additionally, Jambojet has pledged support for contact tracing efforts. The report underscores the importance of a coordinated response and the challenges faced in managing the outbreak. While the article discusses the implications of the case, it does not provide specific details on the number of cases, deaths, or exposures. The focus is on the broader public health and operational response rather than the scale of the outbreak. The Standard Media Group, a leading Kenyan media outlet, reports on the developments, highlighting the urgency of the situation and the need for enhanced measures to combat the virus.

GO TO SITE MSF Access CRASH Based in Paris, CRASH conducts and directs studies and analysis of MSF actions. They participate in internal training sessions and assessment missions in the field. GO TO SITE CRASH UREPH Based in Geneva, UREPH (or Research Unit) aims to improve the way MSF projects are implemented in the field and to participate in critical thinking on humanitarian and medical action. GO TO SITE UREPH ARHP Based in Barcelona, ARHP documents and reflects on the operational challenges and dilemmas faced by the MSF field teams. GO TO SITE ARHP MSF Analysis Based in Brussels, MSF Analysis intends to stimulate reflection and debate on humanitarian topics organised around the themes of migration, refugees, aid access, health policy and the environment in which aid operates. GO TO SITE MSF Analysis MSF Supply This logistical and supply centre in Brussels provides storage of and delivers medical equipment, logistics and drugs for international purchases for MSF missions. GO TO SITE MSF Supply MSF Logistique This supply and logistics centre in Bordeaux, France, provides warehousing and delivery of medical equipment, logistics and drugs for international purchases for MSF missions. GO TO SITE MSF Logistique Amsterdam Procurement Unit This logistical centre in Amsterdam purchases, tests, and stores equipment including vehicles, communications material, power supplies, water-processing facilities and nutritional supplements. GO TO SITE Amsterdam Procurement Unit Brazilian Medical Unit BRAMU specialises in neglected tropical diseases, such as dengue and Chagas, and other infectious diseases. This medical unit is based in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. GO TO SITE Brazilian Medical Unit MSF Medical Guidelines Our medical guidelines are based on scientific data collected from MSF’s experiences, the World Health Organization (WHO), other renowned international medical institutions, and medical and scientific journals. GO TO SITE MSF Medical Guidelines Epicentre Providing epidemiological expertise to underpin our operations, conducting research and training to support our goal of providing medical aid in areas where people are affected by conflict, epidemics, disasters, or excluded from health care. GO TO SITE Epicentre Evaluation Units Evaluation Units have been established in Vienna, Stockholm, and Paris, assessing the potential and limitations of medical humanitarian action, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of our medical humanitarian work. GO TO SITE Evaluation Units LGBTQI+ Inclusion in Health Settings MSF works with LGBTQI+ populations in many settings over the last 25-30 years. LGBTQI+ people face healthcare disparities with limited access to care and higher disease rates than the general population. GO TO SITE LGBTQI+ Inclusion in Health Settings LUXOR The Luxembourg Operational Research (LuxOR) unit coordinates field research projects and operational research training, and provides support for documentation activities and routine data collection. GO TO SITE LUXOR Intersectional Benchmarking Unit The Intersectional Benchmarking Unit collects and analyses data about local labour markets in all locations where MSF employs people. GO TO SITE Intersectional Benchmarking Unit MSF Academy for Healthcare To upskill and provide training to locally-hired MSF staff in several countries, MSF has created the MSF Academy for Healthcare. GO TO SITE MSF Academy for Healthcare Humanitarian Law This Guide explains the terms, concepts, and rules of humanitarian law in accessible and reader-friendly alphabetical entries. GO TO SITE Humanitarian Law MSF Paediatric Days The MSF Paediatric Days is an event for paediatric field staff, policy makers and academia to exchange ideas, align efforts, inspire and share frontline research to advance urgent paediatric issues of direct concern for the humanitarian field. GO TO SITE MSF Paediatric Days MSF Foundation The MSF Foundation aims to create a fertile arena for logistics and medical knowledge-sharing to meet the needs of MSF and the humanitarian sector as a whole. GO TO SITE MSF Foundation DNDi A collaborative, patients’ needs-driven, non-profit drug research and development organisation that is developing new treatments for neglected diseases, founded in 2003 by seven organisations from around the world. GO TO SITE DNDi MSF Science Portal Our digital portal dedicated to sharing the latest medical evidence from our humanitarian activities around the globe. GO TO SITE MSF Science Portal Noma Noma is a preventable and treatable neglected disease, but 90 per cent of people will die within the first two weeks of infection if they do not receive treatment. GO TO SITE Noma TIC The TIC is aiming to change how MSF works to better meet the evolving needs of our patients. GO TO SITE TIC Telemedicine MSF's telemedicine hub aims to overcome geographic barriers for equitable, accessible, and quality patient care. GO TO SITE Telemedicine Sweden Innovation Unit Launched in 2012, the MSF Sweden Innovation Unit deploys a human-centered approach for promoting a culture of innovation within MSF. GO TO SITE Sweden Innovation Unit Geo MSF The GeoMSF platform is a dynamic one-stop-shop website for all of MSF's GIS related services and products. Access maps and applications through the catalogue, request geographical support, or produce a map on GeoMSF. GeoMSF Geo MSF View Resource Centre Conflict in Sudan Why we could not stop cholera in Sudan Women queue to fill their cups with water from a tank at the general healthcare centre in Al-Salam displacement camp. Many families do not have sufficient access to clean drinking water at the camp. The poor water supply poses several risks, including the spread of waterborne diseases, such as cholera and diarrhoea. Sudan, May 2026. © Ante Bussmann/MSF Opinion 6 Oct 2026 In 2024 and 2025, Sudan endured the deadliest cholera outbreak in its modern history. Dr Micaela Serafini, President of MSF in Switzerland, reflects on the lessons learned from the outbreak. Our teams are made up of tens of thousands of health professionals, logistic and administrative staff - most of them hired locally. Our actions are guided by medical ethics and the principles of impartiality, independence and neutrality. In Focus Attacks on medical care Attacks against medical facilities and health workers, whether deliberate or indiscriminate, are part of generalised violence and atrocities committed against civilians in armed conflict. They deprive populations of health services, often when they need them the most. In Focus Conflict in Sudan Find out the latest information on MSF's response to the conflict in Sudan. In Focus Mediterranean migration Every year, thousands of people fleeing war, persecution and poverty at home attempt the treacherous journey across the Mediterranean. Countless lives are lost on the way. In Focus Rohingya refugee crisis Legally stateless, with very limited options or rights in any country where they have sought refuge, the Rohingya are extremely vulnerable. view more video Welcome to Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders Working with MSF What's it like to work with MSF? We rely on a strong network of professionals to deliver life-saving medical aid. Each year, thousands of international and locally-hired staff work together around the globe to provide lifesaving medical assistance to people who would otherwise be denied access to healthcare. news.content_title: Kenya Reports First Case Of Ebola Bundibugyo Virus As Patient Dies In Nairobi | Sahara Reporters
news.content: Skip to main content Social Media Links Search Header Navigation News Opinion More topics Politics Sports Entertainment Education Lifestyle #NigeriaDecides Main navigation Videos Photos Documents Kenya Reports First Case Of Ebola Bundibugyo Virus As Patient Dies In Nairobi October 6, 2026 News According to Tedros, the patient fell ill while in the DRC and received treatment at several hospitals before travelling from the DRC to Nairobi, Kenya, through Kampala, Uganda. The Kenyan government has reported an imported case of Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus in a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, disclosed this in a statement shared on his official X account. According to Tedros, the patient fell ill while in the DRC and received treatment at several hospitals before travelling from the DRC to Nairobi, Kenya, through Kampala, Uganda. He said the patient subsequently died in Nairobi. “The Government of Kenya has reported imported case of Ebola caused by Bundibugyo virus, in a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the DRC,” Tedros said. “The patient became ill in DRC and received treatment in several hospitals, then travelled from DRC to Nairobi via Kampala, Uganda. He died in Nairobi yesterday. “My condolences to his family and loved ones.” The WHO chief said the UN health agency was supporting the governments of Kenya, the DRC and Uganda in response efforts following the reported case. He said the measures include contact tracing, surveillance and screening to identify potential cases and prevent further transmission of the virus. “WHO is supporting the governments of Kenya, the DRC, and Uganda in contact tracing, surveillance, screening, and other response measures to rapidly identify potential cases and prevent further spread of the virus,” he said. Tedros said the WHO was continuing to monitor the situation closely. He also advised against imposing travel or trade restrictions on the affected countries based on the information currently available. The Kenyan government notified WHO of the case on October 6 in line with the International Health Regulations. Kenya is the fourth country to confirm BVD. The Democratic Republic of Congo is currently responding to an outbreak, while Uganda ended its latest outbreak in August 2026. France also reported a travel-related case in June 2026. Kenyan health authorities have so far listed 28 contacts, including family members and health workers who cared for the patient. Authorities are also tracing 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight as the patient, with arrangements being made for follow-up and quarantine of people considered at risk. “WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, the affected countries based on the currently available information,” he said. “We continue to closely monitor and, where necessary, verify travel and trade measures in relation to this epidemic.” The Bundibugyo virus is one of the viruses that causes Ebola disease, a severe illness that can spread through contact with infected bodily fluids. news.title_zh: 肯尼亚报告首例埃博拉本迪布焦病毒病例,患者在内罗毕死亡
news.source_body_en: Kenya has reported its first case of Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus, with the patient dying in Nairobi. The individual had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and received treatment there before traveling through Kampala, Uganda, to Kenya. The Kenyan government notified the World Health Organization (WHO) on October 6, 2026, in line with international health regulations. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus confirmed the case in a statement and emphasized that travel or trade restrictions should not be imposed on the affected countries. Health authorities have identified 28 contacts, including family members and health workers, and are tracing 23 passengers and four crew members on the same flight. The WHO is supporting response efforts in Kenya, the DRC, and Uganda, focusing on contact tracing, surveillance, and screening to prevent further transmission. The situation remains under close monitoring, with no explicit risk level or containment status provided.

Stigmatisation, social exclusion and poverty are all realities that can push some patients to stop taking their treatment. These challenges can also be acute for survivors of sexual violence, street children and sex workers, who are often particularly vulnerable and marginalised in DRC. Murphy Research news Rapid diagnostics and vaccine research strengthen response to outbreak of Ebola's Bundibugyo strain of deadly virus 01 Oct, 2026 by Alan Booth 3 min read Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share on Twitter / X Share via Email Share Subscribe for newsletter updates Researchers have developed a rapid approach to validate diagnostic tests for Bundibugyo virus and found evidence that an existing Zaire ebolavirus vaccine could provide cross-protection, offering potential tools to strengthen responses to the 2026 outbreak The current outbreak of Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has highlighted the difficulties that health authorities face when a rare and dangerous pathogen emerges for which dedicated diagnostic tests, vaccines and treatments are unavailable or at best limited. Two studies led by researchers from the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin and the German Primate Center – Leibniz Institute for Primate Research in Göttingen – including international collaborators – have examined different aspects of the response. The research assessed how diagnostic tests could be evaluated rapidly and whether an established Ebola vaccine might offer some protection against BDBV. During the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers at Charité led by Professor Christian Drosten, a DZIF scientist, rapidly developed a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay for Sars-CoV-2 virus. Its validated design was made publicly available which allowed manufacturers and laboratories to reproduce it and helped to expand testing capacity. European Union legislation has since introduced more stringent requirements for diagnostic devices. Although intended to ensure test performance, these requirements can present difficulties during outbreaks when validated diagnostics are required rapidly and appropriate reference materials are scarce. The 2026 BDBV outbreak provided an opportunity to address this problem. BDBV belongs to the Ebolavirus genus and can cause severe Ebola virus disease but there is no vaccine or therapeutic treatment specifically licensed against it. On 20 May 2026, the Charité hospital admitted a patient from the USA who had contracted BDBV in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Researchers obtained viral genetic material from a throat swab and established a reference standard against which candidate diagnostic assays could be evaluated. The team assembled an international network of nine laboratories that included DZIF members, the German National University Medicine Network (NUM), European research consortia, university hospitals and biosafety level four laboratories – the highest laboratory containment level. The network assessed four candidate PCR tests from two manufacturers. Within two weeks, the laboratories completed analytical and clinical evaluations, with no evidence of cross-reactivity. The results demonstrated that a decentralised network could rapidly generate robust test-performance data to support regulatory assessment and deployment during an infectious disease emergency. The researchers also highlighted the importance of collaboration between publicly funded laboratories and diagnostic manufacturers. Rare pathogens provide relatively little commercial incentive to develop tests that might be required only occasionally, so public investment would be required to maintain preparedness for high-consequence diseases. A second study, led by DZIF scientist Professor Stefan Pöhlmann at the German Primate Center, examined the biological characteristics of the 2026 BDBV strain and whether vaccination against Zaire ebolavirus might offer cross-protection. Researchers focused on the viral glycoprotein, a surface protein that allows ebolaviruses to enter host cells and represents an important target for neutralising antibodies. Because authentic BDBV requires biosafety level four containment, they used pseudovirus particles that carried glycoproteins from BDBV strains associated with outbreaks in 2007–08, 2012 and 2026. The experiments found no evidence that the 2026 glycoprotein allowed more efficient entry into human cells than those from earlier strains. Researchers also examined serum from ten healthy volunteers who had received the licensed recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus-Zaire ebolavirus vaccine, known as rVSV-ZEBOV. Samples were assessed before vaccination and at 28 and 180 days afterwards. After vaccination, antibodies could neutralise pseudoviruses that carried glycoproteins from all three BDBV strains. BDBV-specific neutralising activity was detected in six of the ten vaccine recipients at both post-vaccination time points, although activity was approximately 3.5 to 3.6 times lower than against Zaire ebolavirus. The results provide evidence that antibodies elicited by the licensed vaccine can recognise and inhibit BDBV in laboratory models. However, the researchers cautioned that the experiments did not demonstrate protection against BDBV infection or disease in people because the study used pseudoviruses and measured neutralisation in vitro. Taken together, the studies demonstrate how diagnostic science, virology and immunology can provide complementary tools during an infectious disease outbreak. International laboratory networks, accessible reference materials and regulatory mechanisms established before an emergency could help to reduce the interval between identification of an emerging pathogen and access to reliable diagnostics and potential preventive measures. analysis.time: The outbreak of Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) is reported in 2026, with the publication date of the news being 2026-10-01. The research on diagnostic tests and vaccine cross-protection was conducted during the outbreak.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak of Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) occurred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The research involved an international network of laboratories, including those in Germany and other countries, and focused on BDBV as the target pathogen.
analysis.event: Researchers developed a rapid diagnostic method for Bundibugyo virus and found evidence that a Zaire ebolavirus vaccine could offer cross-protection. This research was conducted during an outbreak of BDBV in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and the findings were reported by the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) and its collaborators.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak of Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo highlighted the challenges of responding to rare pathogens. The research found that six out of ten vaccine recipients showed BDBV-specific neutralising activity, though it was lower than against Zaire ebolavirus. No specific case or death counts were reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The research was conducted to evaluate diagnostic tests and assess vaccine cross-protection. The findings suggest potential tools for responding to the outbreak, but no confirmed or suspected cases were reported in the evidence. The study was part of an international effort to improve preparedness for high-consequence diseases.

analysis.brief_en: In 2026, an outbreak of Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo prompted researchers to develop rapid diagnostic methods and assess the potential cross-protection of an existing Zaire ebolavirus vaccine. The study, led by the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) and international collaborators, demonstrated that a decentralized network of laboratories could generate robust test-performance data during an infectious disease emergency. Six out of ten vaccine recipients showed BDBV-specific neutralising activity, though it was approximately 3.5 to 3.6 times lower than against Zaire ebolavirus. The research highlights the need for public investment in preparedness for rare, high-consequence pathogens. No specific case or death counts were reported in the evidence, and the findings are based on laboratory assessments rather than confirmed outbreak data.

Investigations Obituaries Death Notices Games & Puzzles Align Crossword Mini Crossword KenKen Sudoku Word Flower Horoscopes Business Technology Economy Housing Real Estate Biotech The Fine Print Bold Types Politics Money, Power, Inequality Climate Spotlight Opinion Ideas Columns and Op-eds Editorials Letters Cartoons Say More podcast College Town New Hampshire Business Politics Education Crime Health Commentary Rhode Island Things to Do Rhode Island Podcast RI Food & Dining Politics Business Arts Crime World COVID Globe Magazine The Big Day Dinner with Cupid Perspective Connections Lifestyle A Beautiful Resistance Food & Dining Comics Games Travel Pop Culture Relationships Love Letters Real Estate Arts Books Movies Music TV Visual Arts Performing Arts Cars Real Estate Events Share a News Tip or Story Idea Search Podcasts Newsletters More MetroWeatherPoliticsSportsBusinessPuzzlesRhode IslandGlobe MagazineOpinionHealth careArtsLifestyleEducationCambridge & SomervilleMoney, Power, InequalitySpotlightTechnologyClimateCarsReal EstateEvents Congo’s Ebola outbreak records more than 4,000 deaths as authorities struggle to contain the virus Doctors label the sample collected from an enrolled patient and record it in the hospital's files during clinical trials attempting to stop the rare Bundibugyo virus, amidst a deadly Ebola outbreak, in Rwampara Hospital in Ituri, Congo, on Oct. 1.Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo/Dieudonne Dirole BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Congo’s Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus. The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases, making up for nearly half of the confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. Congo announced an outbreak on May 15, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine. The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots. A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources. The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo’s ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries. Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation’s 17th Ebola outbreak. Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country’s government for reasons ranging from how it’s managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption

OffOn Stream on Kenya records 1st Ebola death after man travels between several countries The patient went through a health screening during his journey, officials said. ByDragana Jovanovic and Mary Kekatos October 6, 2026, 4:03 PM Kenyan health officials confirmed on Tuesday the country's first Ebola death as an outbreak in the nearby Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to spread. The person was a Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for the last seven years, Aden Duale, Kenya's cabinet secretary of health, said in a press conference. The Ministry of Health told ABC News the patient was 40 years old and traveled from Buta, a city in the northwestern DRC. Duale said the patient fell ill about a month ago and was treated in several hospitals while in the DRC. He traveled from the DRC to Kampala, the capital of neighboring Uganda, by road, then boarded a Jambo Jet flight, arriving in Kenyan capital Nairobi last Saturday, Oct. 3. Related Should I hug my children? Ebola doctor on outbreak frontlines faces daily dilemma The patient underwent a public health screening at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport and was taken by a friend to Nairobi Hospital, where he was isolated and later transferred to the East Wing Isolation Facility. Duale said the patient had symptoms including fever, chills, fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, sore throat and painful swallowing. Doctors collected a sample from the patient, which was positive for Ebola and specifically Bundibugyo virus, a rare variant of Ebola behind the current DRC outbreak for which there are no vaccines and no treatments. Kenya Health minister Aden Duale speaks to journalists as he announces the first case of Ebola virus in Kenya, Nairobi, Oct. 6, 2026. Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo Dr. Patrick Amoth, director general for health in Kenya's Ministry of Health, said during the briefing that officials believe the patient knew he was ill and reached out to friends and relatives to transport him from the airport to the hospital directly. "It is potentially possible that some of the medications that he was taking could be able to mask some of the symptoms and therefore give a false positive screening, meaning you could pass through the [airport screening system] because you have taken a medicine, say for example to lower your temperature," Amoth said. "We believe that he knew that he was unwell." Duale said the patient was given supportive treatment but passed away on Monday evening. "We take this opportunity to pass our sincere condolences to the family and friends of the departed. Arrangement for safe and dignified burial of the deceased are ongoing, and the burial is planned for later today in line with the Ebola safe and dignified public health protocols," Duale said. Duale said that 28 contacts of the patient, including family members and healthcare workers who attended to him, have been identified. Health officials are attempting to contact 23 more passengers and four crew members who were on the flight with the patient, and arrangements for quarantine among those at risk have been prepared. Related France confirms 1st Ebola case linked to DRC as UN warns outbreak is fastest-growing in Africa's history "I wish to assure the public not to panic as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease," Duale said. "The public is urged to continue with the frequent hand washing or use of alcoholic hand [wipes] and avoid close contact with sick people coming from countries reporting active transmission of Ebola disease." Popular Reads Vietnamese police arrest 12 suspected of snatching cats for meat 17 hours ago Concerns over Iran drone attack prompted pulling bombers from UK base, sources say 6 hours ago Russia downplays suspected plague case as Trump offers US help 6 hours ago Amoth said Kenyan health officials are collaborating with immediate neighbors and partners including the neighboring country of Uganda, as well as the WHO. "You [are not] able to put a wall between Uganda and [the DRC], between Kenya and Uganda, to prevent the entry of a pathogen," he said. "Therefore, we continue to maintain a heightened state of alert, and what is important for us is to be able to pick [up] the disease when it arrives within our borders, and ensure that we prevent community transmission." People walk outside the Nairobi Hospital where the first Ebola patient had been admitted before he died in Nairobi, Kenya, October 6, 2026. Monicah Mwangi/Reuters Irene Bosire, Kenya deputy director of programs for the humanitarian nonprofit International Rescue Committee, said in a statement that with confirmation of the first imported Ebola case in Kenya, focus has shifted from preparedness to response. "The IRC is working closely with national and county governments, following Kenya's Ebola preparedness and response plan," Bosire said. "We are supporting screening activities to track the disease, trace people who have been in contact with the patient to stop it spreading, share clear information with communities, and provide supplies to prevent infection." As of Oct. 3, 8,854 cases of Ebola and 4,114 deaths have been confirmed, according to the Congo Ministry of Health, with 824 patients in isolation. The case fatality rate currently stands at 48.2% while contact tracing has improved since the summer to 73.8%, the ministry noted. analysis.brief_en: Kenya has recorded its first Ebola death, according to officials. The patient, a Kenyan man who had been living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for seven years, fell ill about a month ago and was treated in several hospitals in the DRC. He traveled to Uganda and then to Nairobi, arriving last Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. Officials have urged the public to maintain hygiene practices and avoid close contact with sick individuals from affected regions.

news.content: Home Animals Biology Environment Health & Medicine Tech Travel Space Natureworldnews.com Let's Connect Trending climate change Earth whales Ebola Outbreak Caused by a Bat-Linked Virus With No Approved Vaccine Passes 4,000 Deaths in Congo By Sydney Anderson Published: Oct 06 2026, 10:00 AM EDT Facebook Twitter Linkedin Comment Mail Kevin J. Olival | EcoHealth Alliance The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has now killed more than 4,000 people. Figures released by Congo's health ministry on Thursday, Oct. 1, show 4,018 deaths among 8,300 confirmed cases, making it the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record, according to CBS News and the Associated Press. What makes this outbreak unusual is the virus behind it. It is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rarer member of the Ebola family for which no vaccine or treatment has been approved. Existing Ebola tools were built for a different species, and doctors are testing them here without proof that they work. The World Health Organization rates the global risk as low, and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says the risk to Americans remains low. But the outbreak is a stark example of how a virus thought to live quietly in wildlife can become a regional emergency when it reaches crowded, conflict-hit communities. A Different Ebola Virus With Fewer Tools Ebola disease is caused by several related viruses named for where they were found. The best known is Zaire ebolavirus, which drove the West African epidemic of 2014 to 2016. For Zaire virus, there is a licensed vaccine, Ervebo, and approved antibody treatments. None of those approvals cover Bundibugyo — not the vaccine and not the antibody drugs. Doctors Without Borders notes that the two monoclonal antibody drugs approved after trials in Congo between 2018 and 2020 are specific to Zaire virus and are not effective or approved for this one. Antiviral and antibody candidates exist, but their efficacy has not been proven in clinical trials. That is why Ervebo is being used here only within research. As of late September, 6,300 health care workers had received the vaccine as part of a clinical trial, and another 1,066 people had also been vaccinated, according to an Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention briefing reported by CIDRAP. The vaccine works against Zaire virus, and its effectiveness against Bundibugyo is still being estimated. Congo is also studying remdesivir as a treatment and obeldesivir to prevent infection after exposure. Without a targeted drug, care relies on basics — fluids, oxygen and close monitoring. Early supportive care can save lives, but many patients reach treatment late. A Death Rate Near One in Two The national case fatality rate stands at 48.4%, according to Africa CDC data cited by CIDRAP. In North Kivu province, it is higher, at 59.3%. Those figures are consistent with what is known about this virus. The World Health Organization reports that the only two earlier Bundibugyo outbreaks, in Uganda in 2007 and Congo in 2012, had fatality rates of 30% and 50%. Bundibugyo disease begins with fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat, which look like malaria or other common illnesses. That makes early detection hard, and patients are not infectious until symptoms begin. Conditions on the ground make everything harder. The outbreak is centered in eastern provinces with years of armed conflict and displacement. On Sept. 27, a ruling-party official was beaten to death in Butembo after urging Ebola prevention on the radio, and days later soldiers searching for weapons burned a camp near Bunia that held an Ebola transit center, forcing 19,000 people to flee, CIDRAP reported. Unpaid health workers have protested and gone on strike. At least 50 health workers have died. Signs of a Slowdown, With Caveats There are hints of progress. The 278 infections confirmed near the end of September were the lowest weekly count since mid-June, and weekly deaths fell to 192 from a peak of 364 in mid-August. More than 21 days have passed without a new case in 18 health zones. Officials warn those numbers may be misleading. Wessam Mankoula, an epidemiologist with Africa CDC, said at the briefing that "this curve doesn't mean that the outbreak is totally under control." Insecurity and community resistance in several hotspots have kept teams from doing surveillance, he said, and contact tracing reaches only about 23% of the expected contacts. The outbreak is also shifting. North Kivu now accounts for nearly 40% of newly confirmed cases, up from 24% at the end of August, according to Doctors Without Borders. A staff member with the group tested positive on Sept. 29 and was flown to the Netherlands for care. The Wildlife Link and What It Means Beyond Congo Bundibugyo is a zoonotic virus, meaning it originated in animals. WHO says fruit bats are suspected to be its natural reservoir. People are thought to become infected through close contact with the blood or body fluids of infected wildlife, such as bats or nonhuman primates, after which the virus spreads between people through bodily fluids, unsafe burials, and gaps in hospital infection control. The sources reviewed for this report do not identify the specific animal source of the 2026 outbreak. For U.S. readers, the CDC says the overall risk to the American public remains low, and the likelihood of Ebola spreading to the United States is very low. No cases linked to this outbreak have been reported in the country. The agency began a public health emergency response on May 17, and WHO, in its June 6 assessment, rated the global risk as low. A case diagnosed in France in June recovered without spreading the virus, and Uganda declared its own outbreak over in July. Travel rules are strict. According to the CDC's Ebola situation page, updated Oct. 1, travelers who have been in Congo within 21 days of their flight are not allowed to board commercial flights to the United States, and U.S. citizens are told to stay outside Congo for 21 days before entering the country. Travelers from Uganda and South Sudan must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. The CDC advises against all travel to Ituri and North Kivu provinces. The next key data will come from WHO situation reports and Africa CDC briefings. Researchers are also waiting on results from the vaccine and treatment trials, which could shape how future Bundibugyo outbreaks are fought. Until then, the response depends on old tools: finding cases, isolating patients, tracing contacts and earning community trust. Congo's health ministry reported 4,018 deaths among 8,300 confirmed cases in figures released on Thursday, Oct. 1. What is Bundibugyo virus? It is one of several viruses that cause Ebola disease. It was first identified in Uganda in 2007, and this is only the third known outbreak it has caused. Is there a vaccine for this Ebola outbreak? No vaccine is approved for the Bundibugyo virus. The Ervebo vaccine, approved for a different Ebola species, is being tested in a clinical trial, mainly among health workers. Why is the death rate so high? About 48% of confirmed cases have died nationally. There is no targeted treatment, early symptoms resemble common illnesses, and conflict delays care and testing. Where does the virus come from? WHO says fruit bats are suspected to be the natural reservoir. Humans can be infected through contact with infected wildlife, then spread it to others through bodily fluids. Is the outbreak slowing down? Weekly confirmed cases and deaths have fallen from their peaks, but Africa CDC warns underreporting in insecure areas may hide ongoing transmission. What does this mean for Americans? The CDC says the risk to the American public is low, and no U.S. cases have been reported. Travelers who were in Congo within the past 21 days cannot board commercial flights to the United States, and the agency advises against all travel to Ituri and North Kivu provinces. news.source_body_en: An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, has now resulted in over 4,000 deaths, making it the fastest-growing outbreak on record. The virus, which has no approved vaccine or treatment, spreads through close contact with infected wildlife and human-to-human transmission. As of late September 2026, 8,300 cases were confirmed, with a national case fatality rate of 48.4% and 59.3% in North Kivu. The World Health Organization and U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have rated the risk to the American public as low, with no cases linked to this outbreak in the U.S. Response efforts include the use of the Zaire ebolavirus vaccine in research settings and early supportive care, though challenges persist due to insecurity and community resistance. The outbreak is centered in eastern provinces, where armed conflict and displacement have complicated containment. Despite some signs of a slowdown, officials warn that the situation remains uncertain, with contact tracing reaching only about 23% of expected contacts.
news.content_zh: 刚果民主共和国由本迪布焦病毒引起的埃博拉病毒 暴发 目前已导致 4,000 多人死亡,成为有记录以来增长最快的埃博拉病毒 暴发。该病毒尚未获得批准的 疫苗 或 治疗,通过与受感染的野生动物和人际接触 传播 进行传播。截至2026年9月下旬,确诊病例8,300例,全国病死率为48.4%,北基伍省为59.3%。世界卫生组织和美国疾病控制与预防中心已将美国公众面临的风险评为较低,美国没有与该 暴发 有关的病例。应对工作包括在研究环境和早期支持性护理中使用扎伊尔埃博拉病毒 疫苗,但由于不安全和社区抵制,挑战仍然存在。暴发以东部省份为中心,武装冲突和流离失所问题的遏制十分复杂。尽管出现了一些放缓的迹象,但官员们警告说,情况仍然不确定,接触者追踪仅达到预期接触者的 23% 左右。

Ebola outbreak shows that the world is not ready for the next pandemic By Olivia Ndubuisi A woman walks past a poster about Ebola prevention in Mambasa, Ituri, Democratic Republic of Congo, 24 August 2026 (Keystone/EPA/Dieudonné Dirole) As Ebola continues to spread in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, the burning question at recent UN pandemic preparedness meetings at the UN General Assembly was: Is the world willing and able to pay for readiness? When the Marburg virus hit Rwanda in September 2024, the country’s No. 1 goal was stopping community transmission. Marburg, in the same family as the Ebola virus, is second among the top-four deadliest viruses in the world. More than 80 per cent of people who contract the disease die. The country tracked the source of the zoonotic disease, and using genomic sequencing, sequenced the virus. They discovered that the outbreak was closely related to a sequence that happened in an outbreak of Marburg in Uganda in 2014. Rwanda mounted an ambitious response by beginning contact tracing, mass testing and surveillance. Ultimately, 9.6 million people were screened by about 54,000 community health workers. From the diagnosis of the first case of Marburg to the deployment of the first shot of the experimental Sabin Vaccine Institute inoculation was 10 days. The case fatality rate for the outbreak stayed at 22 per cent, the lowest ever recorded for the virus. Two years on, across the border from Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), has entered Day 139 of its fight against a new strain of an Ebola outbreak, called Bundibugyo. Approximately 3,700 people have died since the outbreak was declared in mid-May 2026. The first encouraging signs of progress to fight it may be emerging. Rwanda’s response to the Marburg outbreak, hailed the world over, was possible because the country had spent years preparing for such an epidemic. But the DRC is trying to build responses in altogether different conditions: It is coping with a humanitarian crisis amid a war. So the burning question that dominated the UN’s pandemic preparedness meetings at the General Assembly high-level session last week was: Is the world willing and able to pay for readiness now? On the ground in DRC According to the WHO, from 31 August to 20 September, the cases of Ebola in the DRC declined by approximately 26 per cent at the epicenter, Ituri Province. However, in the same period, North Kivu Province, near Ituri, recorded a 73 per cent increase, evidence that the outbreak was evolving across the numerous affected areas. “Each of the seven affected provinces has its own transmission pattern. One of our greatest concerns is that too many people are still dying before reaching treatment,” said Dr. Marie Roseline Belizaire, the regional emergency director for WHO Africa. She was speaking by Zoom at a recent UN briefing on the Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC and emergency preparedness ahead of El Niño and other health emergencies in the region. “Every death in the community also increases the risk of further transmission among family members, caregivers, and others involved in burial practices, and although adults account for most confirmed cases,” Dr. Belizaire added. “Children are especially vulnerable.” On the ground in the DRC, she said that all response teams are working closely with communities to identify suspected cases quickly and to address the misinformation that is keeping people from seeking appropriate care. The bigger emphasis has been moving the response away from major urban centers into rural areas, where the most-worrying epidemiologic trends are occurring. The needs are enormous. Money, time and a plan “The problem is multifaceted,” Dr. Catherine Smallwood, a WHO incident manager for the Ebola response in North Kivu, said in the recent UN event. “There is the access one, and there’s also the issue of funding. We need partners. We need time, we need money, we have a plan, and if we really, truly want to be able to stop this epidemic in the next six months, we will need additional resources.” For both Rwanda and the DRC, the realities of fighting the Bundibugyo strain are vastly distinct. Rwanda’s health minister, Yvan Butera, spoke at an event during the UN high-level week hosted by the Pandemic Fund, which focuses on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response in low- and middle-income countries, and the governments of Armenia and Rwanda. The forum spotlighted how countries are investing their own resources to close critical preparedness gaps. Butera said that building a readiness-response plan cannot be done in the middle of a war and humanitarian disaster. The DRC’s effort to control the Ebola outbreak is still lacking an approved vaccine. Provisions of other essential health services are also being carried out under sometimes deadly circumstances. The services include maternal health, routine immunizations, treatments of malaria and other baseline conditions resulting from widespread displacement of civilians. The decades-long conflict in the eastern DRC involves the M23 militia from Rwanda fighting Congolese troops in competition for the area’s mineral wealth. The violence has made the Ebola outbreak hard to contain. As of 30 September 2026, data from the Congolese authorities confirmed a total of 3,901 deaths out of 8,067 confirmed cases in the DRC from the outbreak. It has surpassed previous records to become the largest Ebola outbreak in the history of the DRC, but it has not spread to Rwanda. In May 2026, it spread into neighboring Uganda through infected cross-border travelers, but its government halted transmission and was officially declared virus-free by the WHO in August 2026. Lessons from Covid-19 Six years ago, the Covid-19 pandemic devastated global health systems, and many countries have yet to fully recover. Mathematical modeling by the Center for Global Development, a nongovernmental organization focused on reducing poverty, suggests that the likelihood of another pandemic of the same scale as Covid within the next 25 years will hit nearly 70 percent. Many global health experts believe the odds are climbing closer to a full certainty. But the world moves on too quickly, said Wessam Mankoula, the acting head of Emergency Preparedness and Response Division for Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or Africa CDC. “SARS is over and we forgot, Covid-19 came, we’ve forgotten the devastation,” Mankoula said in a panel on building resilience during last week’s UN General Assembly session. “We need to invest more to build resilient systems now. When the Marburg virus hit Rwanda in September 2024, the country’s No. 1 goal was stopping community transmission. Marburg, in the same family as the Ebola virus, is second among the top-four deadliest viruses in the world. More than 80 per cent of people who contract the disease die. The country tracked the source of the zoonotic disease, and using genomic sequencing, sequenced the virus. They discovered that the outbreak was closely related to a sequence that happened in an outbreak of Marburg in Uganda in 2014. Rwanda mounted an ambitious response by beginning contact tracing, mass testing and surveillance. Ultimately, 9.6 million people were screened by about 54,000 community health workers. From the diagnosis of the first case of Marburg to the deployment of the first shot of the experimental Sabin Vaccine Institute inoculation was 10 days. The case fatality rate for the outbreak stayed at 22 per cent, the lowest ever recorded for the virus. Two years on, across the border from Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), has entered Day 139 of its fight against a new strain of an Ebola outbreak, called Bundibugyo. Approximately 3,700 people have died since the outbreak was declared in mid-May 2026. The first encouraging signs of progress to fight it may be emerging. Rwanda’s response to the Marburg outbreak, hailed the world over, was possible because the country had spent years preparing for such an epidemic.
