She was speaking by Zoom at a recent UN briefing on the Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC and emergency preparedness ahead of El Niño and other health emergencies in the region. “Every death in the community also increases the risk of further transmission among family members, caregivers, and others involved in burial practices, and although adults account for most confirmed cases,” Dr. Belizaire added. “Children are especially vulnerable.” On the ground in the DRC, she said that all response teams are working closely with communities to identify suspected cases quickly and to address the misinformation that is keeping people from seeking appropriate care. Published 6 October 2026 Read am in 4 mins Add am as preferred source for Google Kenya don confam dia first ever case of Ebola for di body of one Kenyan citizen wey bin dey live for di Democratic Republic of Congo for di past seven years. Health Minister Aden Duale tok say di patient, wey fall sick one month ago, and wey dem don treat for several hospitals for DR Congo, die days afta e land Nairobi. Duale explain say di patient bin board one flight on Saturday and e go through normal public screening for di main airport for Nairobi, bifor one of im relative transfer am go one hospital for di city. More dan 4,000 pipo don die from Ebola for DR Congo dis year, for inside wetin be di second-deadliest known outbreak of di disease. However, di World Health Organization (WHO) bin declare di kontri free from di disease for August. Since den, dem dey report all di cases of di disease for DR Congo. Di current outbreak come from di Bundibugyo species of Ebola, wey no too common and currently no get any known vaccine. According to di minister, di patient bin first travel by road from DR Congo go Uganda capital, Kampala, wia e board flight go Nairobi. Duale say afta dem carry di patient go Nairobi Hospital, dem later transfer am go one isolation facility wey dem build during di Covid-19 period. Na dia di patient "develop fever, chills, serious tiredness and weakness, painful swallowing, muscle pain and bleeding under di skin". "Doctors suspect viral haemorrhagic fever based on im symptoms and travel history and collect samples for testing. Di sample test positive for Ebola Bundibugyo virus," Duale tok. Di patient die at 23:30 (20:30 GMT) on Monday and dem plan to bury am later on Tuesday according to public health safety protocols. At least 28 contacts, including family members and healthcare workers, don dey identified, while health authorities dey trace anoda 23 passengers and four crew members wey travel on di same flight. So far, WHO don record 4,082 deaths out of 8,463 cases since di emergence of di Bundibugyo species of di virus. Currently, no approved vaccine or treatment dey for di species, wey dey highly infectious. Medical charity MSF believe say di current toll fit even dey higher becos of gaps of surveillance and testing for di war-torn kontri. On Monday, MSF bin say di virus dey spread "like megafire", wit new hotspots wey dey emerge from North Kivu province, wey border Ituri where the virus began. analysis.brief_en: Kenya has confirmed its first death from Ebola, marking the first known case of the disease in the country. The patient, a Kenyan citizen who had lived in the Democratic Republic of Congo for seven years, fell ill one month ago and was treated in DR Congo before arriving in Nairobi. Health Minister Aden Duale announced the death, stating the patient tested positive for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola virus. The patient died at 23:30 on Monday and was transferred to an isolation facility built during the Covid-19 period. At least 28 contacts have been identified, and authorities are tracing an additional 23 passengers and four crew members from the same flight. The Bundibugyo virus, which has caused over 4,082 deaths out of 8,463 cases in DR Congo since its emergence, remains highly infectious with no approved vaccine or treatment. The World Health Organization declared Kenya free from Ebola in August 2026, but the current outbreak is linked to DR Congo, where the virus is spreading rapidly. The situation highlights the ongoing challenges of managing Ebola outbreaks in regions with limited healthcare resources.

Facebook Twitter Print Email Ebola response faces setback as transit centre burns down in DR Congo camp 1 October 2026 Peace and Security The enormous challenge of halting the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) just became even harder after a key transit centre for patients requiring treatment burned down in Ituri province. Condemning the blaze, the UN’s senior Ebola response official in DRC, Julien Harneis, also noted that Kigonze camp where the facility was open now lies abandoned. “It’s been a huge struggle to create Ebola transit centres [and] Ebola treatment centres; it’s required money, bringing in staff and it’s been a struggle all across the east,” Mr. Harneis told UN News. “So, when we lose a centre, that means we lose capacity, we lose investment and we have to start again. And above all, it means that people do not get access to the care that they really need.” Tweet URL Deserted shelters The camp had provided shelter for some 19,000 people fleeing violence in the resource-rich east of the country, close to the border with Rwanda. In recent days, thousands of people fled Kigonze following reports that soldiers had entered the site searching for weapons and people suspected of belonging to non-State armed groups. Gunfire was also reportedly heard. Describing the transit centre fire on Tuesday evening as “deeply disappointing”, Mr. Harneis explained that staff there had provided “essential and excellent” services to those who needed them. He added that the UN is working with authorities to ensure that health facilities are protected. In related developments, more than 3,000 people fled Rhoe displacement camp in Djugu territory (also in Ituri province) following clashes that intensified on 27 September. According to the UN aid coordination office, OCHA, at least four people were reportedly killed and seven injured, while several houses were burned down in Blukwa. Women and children account for most of those displaced, according to humanitarian sources. Fighting has also severely hampered the Ebola response and restricted humanitarian access to several health zones, including Ituri province’s Fataki, Drodro and Lita. Ongoing insecurity has also delayed the transport of laboratory samples from Fataki to Bunia and disrupted the transfer of confirmed Ebola patients for treatment. Some aid organizations have suspended activities in affected areas. Soundcloud North Kivu responders killed Meanwhile, in neighbouring North Kivu province, two people involved in the Ebola response were reportedly killed in Lubero on 27 and 28 September. Fighting in Masisi has displaced more than 24,000 people since mid-September. OCHA and humanitarian partners are monitoring the situation and calling on all parties to protect civilians, safeguard displacement camps and ensure humanitarian access. Violence has also been reported in South Kivu and Tanganyika provinces of DRC, forcing thousands more people from their homes and increasing humanitarian needs, the aid office said in an update earlier this week. A vast outbreak Ebola has spread across seven provinces since the public health emergency was declared in mid-May. It is the country’s 17th outbreak. The affected provinces are Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, South Ubangi and Tshopo. More than 8,000 cases of infection have been confirmed including 4,000 deaths. Ituri remains the epicentre of the current emergency, with most cases in and around the cities of Bunia and Mongbwalu. In an update, the UN World Health Organization (WHO) stressed the double challenge for Ebola responders – including safe burial teams – who urgently need more help: “Where transmission remains intense, we need to increase capacity to halt the pace of infections. And in emerging hotspots, we need to intervene quickly to stop the virus from taking hold,” the agency said. How the UN is helping WHO is a key supporter of local health authorities, providing assistance with case management, surveillance, safe and dignified burials and community engagement. This is the case in Ituri’s Mongala health region, where 346 confirmed cases of Ebola have now been confirmed, with 149 deaths, since the first infection was detected on 18 May. Located 45 kilometres from the provincial capital, Bunia, access remains difficult and takes nearly two hours by car. Because Mongala lacks a treatment centre, patients are either referred to Nizi – 27 kilometres away – or Bunia, depending on where beds are available and the patient’s choice. In an update, WHO noted that the number of mobile safe and dignified burial teams has increased from 53 teams of 12 members to 114 teams deployed across Ituri province. In areas of high transmission, 57 community teams trained in safe and dignified burials were deployed across 11 health areas in Mongala and Fataki. The number of patient beds has increased too, with the aim of providing more than 1,800 beds across 54 health facilities in 34 health zones. “However, more than 1,400 additional health professionals are needed to support this expansion,” the agency stressed. “Increasing capacity allows us to admit more patients under better conditions and reduce delays. Rapid isolation and treatment of cases is essential,” said Dr Stéphane Mutombo, anaesthaesiologist and resuscitator, head of the clinical component within the holistic care pillar, for DRC’s Ministry of Health. This Ebola outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus. It has become the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in DRC, surpassing the 2018–2020 emergency. It is second only to the 2014–2016 Ebola epidemic in West Africa, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000 in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. analysis.time: The event occurred on 1 October 2026, with the transit centre fire taking place on Tuesday evening. The outbreak has been ongoing since mid-May 2026, and recent clashes intensified on 27 September 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The incident took place in Kigonze camp, Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The affected population includes displaced people, primarily women and children, and the broader population in Ituri province, which has been the epicentre of the outbreak. The outbreak has spread across seven provinces, including Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, South Ubangi, and Tshopo.
analysis.event: A transit centre for Ebola patients in Kigonze camp, Ituri province, burned down, causing the facility to be abandoned. This incident is part of the ongoing challenges in the DRC's Ebola response, with violence and clashes disrupting efforts. The outbreak has resulted in over 8,000 confirmed cases and 4,000 deaths since mid-May 2026.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has affected over 8,000 people with 4,000 deaths. The transit centre fire in Kigonze camp has significantly reduced capacity and access to care. Fighting in Ituri province and other areas has delayed transport of samples and restricted humanitarian access, increasing the risk of further spread. The WHO has emphasized the need for more capacity and intervention in high-transmission areas.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The UN and WHO are working to protect health facilities and increase capacity, including deploying more burial teams and beds. However, the situation remains under investigation, with ongoing clashes and insecurity hampering response efforts. The UN aid coordination office, OCHA, is monitoring the situation and calling for protection of civilians and displacement camps.

analysis.brief_en: A transit centre for Ebola patients in Kigonze camp, Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), burned down on 1 October 2026, causing the facility to be abandoned. This incident has worsened the already difficult Ebola response in the DRC, where violence and clashes have disrupted efforts since mid-May 2026. The outbreak has affected over 8,000 people, resulting in 4,000 deaths, with Ituri province being the epicentre. Fighting in the region has delayed sample transport and restricted humanitarian access, increasing the risk of further spread. The UN and WHO are working to expand capacity, including deploying more burial teams and beds, but the situation remains challenging. OCHA is monitoring the situation and urging protection of civilians and displacement camps.

analysis_en.time: The event occurred on 1 October 2026, with the transit centre fire taking place on Tuesday evening. The outbreak has been ongoing since mid-May 2026, and recent clashes intensified on 27 September 2026.
analysis_en.location_and_population: The incident took place in Kigonze camp, Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The affected population includes displaced people, primarily women and children, and the broader population in Ituri province, which has been the epicentre of the outbreak. The outbreak has spread across seven provinces, including Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, South Ubangi, and Tshopo.
analysis_en.event: A transit centre for Ebola patients in Kigonze camp, Ituri province, burned down, causing the facility to be abandoned. This incident is part of the ongoing challenges in the DRC's Ebola response, with violence and clashes disrupting efforts. The outbreak has resulted in over 8,000 confirmed cases and 4,000 deaths since mid-May 2026.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has affected over 8,000 people with 4,000 deaths. The transit centre fire in Kigonze camp has significantly reduced capacity and access to care. Fighting in Ituri province and other areas has delayed transport of samples and restricted humanitarian access, increasing the risk of further spread. The WHO has emphasized the need for more capacity and intervention in high-transmission areas.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The UN and WHO are working to protect health facilities and increase capacity, including deploying more burial teams and beds. However, the situation remains under investigation, with ongoing clashes and insecurity hampering response efforts. The UN aid coordination office, OCHA, is monitoring the situation and calling for protection of civilians and displacement camps.

Kenya is the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in eastern DR Congo in mid-May. Issued on: 06/10/2026 - 17:41Modified: 06/10/2026 - 18:10 3 min Reading time Share By: FRANCE 24 People with masks leave The Nairobi Hospital, where Kenya's first Ebola virus patient was treated and died, October 6, 2026. © Andrew Kasuku, AP A Kenyan citizen who had been living in Congo before returning to Nairobi over the weekend became Kenya’s first confirmed case of Ebola and the country’s first death from the disease in the fast-moving outbreak, authorities said Tuesday, sparking urgent contact-tracing efforts to try to contain the spread of the virus. The man had been residing in Congo for the past seven years and fell ill about a month ago. He was treated at various hospitals before travelling by road to Kampala, Uganda, where he boarded a flight to the Kenyan capital, arriving on Saturday afternoon, Health Minister Aden Duale said. Health authorities in Kenya have placed the country’s border points on high alert and are monitoring for possible additional cases. Duale said that the man had been isolated and treated at Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for the Ebola virus and died late Monday. Ebola is highly contagious and spreads in the human population through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The current outbreak was declared in mid-May, months after it had been spreading in a remote part of eastern Congo. At least 8,400 cases have been recorded, including more than 4,000 deaths, according to government data, making it the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in history. Kenya has never had an outbreak of Ebola, according to the Kenya Medical Research Institute. The country hosts a United States-funded isolation center for American citizens exposed to Ebola to quarantine for 21 days before travelling back to the US. The isolation facility faced legal battles and deadly protests by locals who feared it was exposing them to the virus. Kenya is the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in eastern Congo in mid-May. Uganda has recorded 20 cases and France, one. Before Kenya reported its case, there had been no active cases outside Congo since Uganda declared its outbreak over in late August. Duale said that 28 contacts of the man who had returned on Saturday – including family members and health workers who cared for the patient – had been identified. Another 23 passengers on the flight and four crew members, who travelled on the same plane from Uganda, were being traced. The contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be released after testing negative for the virus, said the ministry’s director-general, Dr. Patrick Amoth. After the man arrived in Nairobi, his relatives later took him in a private vehicle to Nairobi Hospital, where he was immediately isolated. He will be buried within 24 hours in accordance with recommended public safety protocols. The minister said that Kenya had tested 267 samples at five laboratories across the country since May before this first case was detected. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Tuesday commended the “rapid identification, isolation and testing of the patient” and said a high-level team had been dispatched to Kenya to offer support. In Congo, where the outbreak has spread to seven provinces, conditions are difficult. Responders have faced attacks on health teams, misinformation about the virus, a failure by locals to report symptoms and rebel violence that has limited access to treatment centres. While cases have slowed in Ituri province, the epicentre, the outbreak is spreading in emerging hot spots in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces. “It is like fighting a megafire. Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations,” Stéphanie Hoffmann with Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said in a statement. The World Health Organisation has warned that it could surpass the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history, which erupted more than a decade ago and killed more than 11,000 people in West Africa. Photograph: Daniel Irungu/EPA View image in fullscreen Volunteer health workers at an Ebola emergency response training session conducted by Médecins Sans Frontières in Ongata Rongai, Kenya, in August. Photograph: Daniel Irungu/EPA Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May. This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment. A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters. The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October. Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August. Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”. He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, but “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT). Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”. He added that authorities were looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said. Duale said a “safe and dignified burial” of the man had been planned for later in the day, in line with public health standards, but did not give further details. Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year to allow the US to set up an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi. After starting in the DRC’s north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the country’s north and east. DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak Read more The response to the virus in the vast central African country has been hindered by instability, including clashes between armed groups, mistrust of authorities – which has led to violence against health workers and other officials – and a lack of resources amid huge cuts in international aid. The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. The province now accounts for 40% of all new Ebola cases, compared with 24% at the end of August, the NGO said. “It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.” The wider Butembo health zone is home to around 2 million people and only has four Ebola treatment centres, two of which only opened recently, MSF said. Hoffman said: “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment.” North Kivu is particularly affected by conflict, with 134 violent incidents there in the past month, according to tracking group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, more than any other province. He added that authorities were looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said. Duale said a “safe and dignified burial” of the man had been planned for later in the day, in line with public health standards, but did not give further details. Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year to allow the US to set up an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi. After starting in the DRC’s north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the country’s north and east. DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak Read more The response to the virus in the vast central African country has been hindered by instability, including clashes between armed groups, mistrust of authorities – which has led to violence against health workers and other officials – and a lack of resources amid huge cuts in international aid. The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. The province now accounts for 40% of all new Ebola cases, compared with 24% at the end of August, the NGO said. “It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.” The wider Butembo health zone is home to around 2 million people and only has four Ebola treatment centres, two of which only opened recently, MSF said. Hoffman said: “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment.” North Kivu is particularly affected by conflict, with 134 violent incidents there in the past month, according to tracking group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, more than any other province. news.content_title: Ebola: What are the symptoms, how does it spread and where did it come from?
news.content: Ebola outbreaks emerge periodically in several African countries, most notably in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Public health expert Yap Boum, who has been involved in managing Ebola outbreaks in the past, answers some key questions about Ebola’s history, treatment, and how to keep safe. What are the origins of the virus? Ebola is an old and deadly disease that was discovered in 1976 near the Ebola river in northern DRC. The virus was named after the river. It was discovered by scientists including Jean-Jacques Muyembe – a Congolese microbiologist and general director of the DRC Institut National pour la Recherche Biomedicale – and researchers from the Institute of Tropical Medicine, including Stefaan Pattyn, Guido van der Groen and Peter Piot. Professor Muyembe was called to the village of Yambuku in northern Zaire (now DRC) where a mysterious illness had broken out. He took a sample and sent it to the Institute of Tropical Medicine laboratory in Belgium, where the virus was isolated. Since then, there have been five identified Ebola virus strains, four of which are known to cause disease in humans: Ebola virus (Zaire ebolavirus); Sudan virus (Sudan ebolavirus); Taï Forest virus (Taï Forest ebolavirus, formerly Côte d'Ivoire ebolavirus); and Bundibugyo virus (Bundibugyo ebolavirus). It’s a zoonotic disease (animal-borne) though the natural reservoir host of Ebola virus remains unknown. However, bats are the most likely reservoir. What are the symptoms of Ebola? While the signs and symptoms may appear between 2 and 21 days after contact with the virus, they usually appear between 8 and 10 days. They are quite similar to many tropical diseases, especially malaria and typhoid fever, with which they share symptoms such as: - fever - aches and pains, such as severe headache and muscle and joint pain - weakness and fatigue - sore throat - loss of appetite - abdominal pain - diarrhoea and vomiting - unexplained haemorrhaging, bleeding or bruising. The main differences appear in the late stages of infection. These symptoms might include red eyes, skin rash and hiccups. Can it be treated? The Ebola virus disease can now be treated. The PALM clinical trial – implemented between 2018 and 2020 in the DRC – has evaluated four drug candidates. Two of them – Inmazeb and Ebanga – were approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in October and December 2020 to treat the Ebola virus disease caused by the Ebola virus. They are made available to patients by the World Health Organization (WHO) during Ebola outbreaks and aren’t available in the market. Inmazeb is a combination of three monoclonal antibodies and Ebanga is a single monoclonal antibody. Monoclonal antibodies (often abbreviated as mAbs) are proteins produced in a lab or other manufacturing facility that act like natural antibodies to stop a germ such as a virus from replicating after it has infected a person. Ebanga was isolated from a human survivor of the 1995 Ebola outbreak in Kikwit in the DRC who maintained circulating antibodies against the Ebola virus for more than a decade after infection. Without treatment the average case fatality rate is approximately 50%. But it has ranged from 25% to 90% in past outbreaks. Can it be prevented? People can be vaccinated against one strain, the Zaire Ebola virus. It became a preventable disease following the validation of one vaccine candidate during the Ca Suffit Ebola clinical trial in 2015 in Guinea. The Ebola vaccine rVSV-ZEBOV (called Ervebo®) was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in December 2019. This vaccine is given as a single dose vaccine and has been found to be safe and protective with a reported 100% efficacy. Though it has not yet been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, Johnson & Johnson has a two-dose vaccine for the Zaire strain that was used under emergency use in 2019 during an Ebola outbreak in the DRC. This vaccine requires an initial dose and a “booster” dose 56 days later and could be made available through the WHO during outbreaks. How can you protect yourself? Ebola is a highly transmissible disease but, aside from vaccination for the Zaire strain, its spread can be prevented through behavioural measures. People should avoid contact with blood and body fluids – such as urine, faeces, saliva, sweat, vomit, breast milk, amniotic fluid, semen and vaginal fluids – of people who are sick. People should also avoid contact with their personal items which might have traces of these fluids. People who were previously infected can still carry the disease in their semen. Experience in West Africa shows these burial practices to be among the super spreaders of the Ebola virus. Ebola virus disease is a deadly disease that is preventable and curable. The next step is the local production of diagnostics, vaccines and drugs to ensure that endemic countries control their own stock and can make them available to their population. news.content_original: Ebola outbreaks emerge periodically in several African countries, most notably in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Public health expert Yap Boum, who has been involved in managing Ebola outbreaks in the past, answers some key questions about Ebola’s history, treatment, and how to keep safe. What are the origins of the virus? Ebola is an old and deadly disease that was discovered in 1976 near the Ebola river in northern DRC. The virus was named after the river. It was discovered by scientists including Jean-Jacques Muyembe – a Congolese microbiologist and general director of the DRC Institut National pour la Recherche Biomedicale – and researchers from the Institute of Tropical Medicine, including Stefaan Pattyn, Guido van der Groen and Peter Piot. Professor Muyembe was called to the village of Yambuku in northern Zaire (now DRC) where a mysterious illness had broken out. He took a sample and sent it to the Institute of Tropical Medicine laboratory in Belgium, where the virus was isolated. Since then, there have been five identified Ebola virus strains, four of which are known to cause disease in humans: Ebola virus (Zaire ebolavirus); Sudan virus (Sudan ebolavirus); Taï Forest virus (Taï Forest ebolavirus, formerly Côte d'Ivoire ebolavirus); and Bundibugyo virus (Bundibugyo ebolavirus). It’s a zoonotic disease (animal-borne) though the natural reservoir host of Ebola virus remains unknown. However, bats are the most likely reservoir. What are the symptoms of Ebola? While the signs and symptoms may appear between 2 and 21 days after contact with the virus, they usually appear between 8 and 10 days. They are quite similar to many tropical diseases, especially malaria and typhoid fever, with which they share symptoms such as: - fever - aches and pains, such as severe headache and muscle and joint pain - weakness and fatigue - sore throat - loss of appetite - abdominal pain - diarrhoea and vomiting - unexplained haemorrhaging, bleeding or bruising. The main differences appear in the late stages of infection. These symptoms might include red eyes, skin rash and hiccups. Can it be treated? The Ebola virus disease can now be treated. The PALM clinical trial – implemented between 2018 and 2020 in the DRC – has evaluated four drug candidates. Two of them – Inmazeb and Ebanga – were approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in October and December 2020 to treat the Ebola virus disease caused by the Ebola virus. They are made available to patients by the World Health Organization (WHO) during Ebola outbreaks and aren’t available in the market. Inmazeb is a combination of three monoclonal antibodies and Ebanga is a single monoclonal antibody. Monoclonal antibodies (often abbreviated as mAbs) are proteins produced in a lab or other manufacturing facility that act like natural antibodies to stop a germ such as a virus from replicating after it has infected a person. Ebanga was isolated from a human survivor of the 1995 Ebola outbreak in Kikwit in the DRC who maintained circulating antibodies against the Ebola virus for more than a decade after infection. Without treatment the average case fatality rate is approximately 50%. But it has ranged from 25% to 90% in past outbreaks. Can it be prevented? People can be vaccinated against one strain, the Zaire Ebola virus. It became a preventable disease following the validation of one vaccine candidate during the Ca Suffit Ebola clinical trial in 2015 in Guinea. The Ebola vaccine rVSV-ZEBOV (called Ervebo®) was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in December 2019. This vaccine is given as a single dose vaccine and has been found to be safe and protective with a reported 100% efficacy. Though it has not yet been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, Johnson & Johnson has a two-dose vaccine for the Zaire strain that was used under emergency use in 2019 during an Ebola outbreak in the DRC. This vaccine requires an initial dose and a “booster” dose 56 days later and could be made available through the WHO during outbreaks. How can you protect yourself? Ebola is a highly transmissible disease but, aside from vaccination for the Zaire strain, its spread can be prevented through behavioural measures. People should avoid contact with blood and body fluids – such as urine, faeces, saliva, sweat, vomit, breast milk, amniotic fluid, semen and vaginal fluids – of people who are sick. People should also avoid contact with their personal items which might have traces of these fluids. People who were previously infected can still carry the disease in their semen. Because it’s a zoonotic disease – that is, transmitted from animal to humans – people should avoid contact with bats, forest antelopes, nonhuman primates (such as monkeys and chimpanzees) and wild meat and blood especially in endemic areas. Lastly, funeral or burial practices that involve touching the body of someone who may have died from Ebola should be avoided. Experience in West Africa shows these burial practices to be among the super spreaders of the Ebola virus. Ebola virus disease is a deadly disease that is preventable and curable. The next step is the local production of diagnostics, vaccines and drugs to ensure that endemic countries control their own stock and can make them available to their population. Africa can’t be left behind once more when it comes to diagnostics, vaccines and treatment, as it has been during the COVID pandemic and monkeypox outbreaks. news.content_title: Ebola kills first victim in Kenya as deadly disease hits FOURTH country after infected patient boarded flight from Congo
news.content: EBOLA has killed its first victim in Kenya as the deadly disease hits its fourth country after an infected passenger boarded a flight from Congo. The Kenyan man died in Nairobi late on Monday after travelling from the Democratic Republic of Congo where the virus has already killed more than 4,000 people. Ebola has killed its first victim as the deadly disease hits its third country Credit: AFP Health Minister Aden Duale confirmed Kenya’s first ever case on Tuesday Credit: Shutterstock Editorial His death marks Kenya’s first-ever recorded case of Ebola and has sparked an urgent hunt for dozens of people who may have come into contact with him. Health chiefs are now scrambling to trace 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight from Uganda – a connecting flight to Nairobi – on Saturday. Sign up for The US Sun newsletter Thank you! Another 28 contacts – including relatives and medics who cared for the victim – have already been identified and face 21 days of isolation. Health Minister Aden Duale said that so far “only one test has turned out positive,” referring to the dead unnamed man from Kenya . Kenyan border points have also been placed on high alert amid fears the highly contagious killer could spread further. Despite the dramatic escalation, Duale urged terrified Kenyans “not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease”. It comes as the outbreak rips through eastern Congo at alarming speed, with health workers battling what one expert described as a viral “megafire”. At least 8,463 cases have now been confirmed in Congo, with 4,082 deaths – making it the country’s largest ever recorded Ebola outbreak. Facebook Twitter Print Email ‘Ebola takes the people children depend on’: UNICEF 6 October 2026 Health The Ebola outbreak in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is robbing children of their loved ones – with some succumbing to the deadly disease themselves, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) reported on Tuesday. The update comes as regional neighbour Kenya confirmed its first case and death from the disease, believed to have come from DRC. “Ebola takes the people children depend on and unravels their lives,” said Halimatou Amadou, UNICEF Chief of Communication in the DRC, speaking to journalists in Geneva. “The parents fall ill, a child may be exposed, the parent is taken for treatment or dies. At the very moment a child most needs someone, fear and stigma can keep relatives and neighbours away.” Nearly 2,000 children affected More than 1,900 boys and girls have either lost one or both parents, or their caregivers, since the outbreak was declared in May, or have been separated from them. Most of these children, 1,581, are in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis. A further 322 are in neighbouring North Kivu province. “And these are the children we know about because these figures cover only the area where UNICEF works with social affairs teams in the affected provinces,” she said. Fighters and survivors Ms. Amadou put names behind the numbers, such as Lina*, a seven-month-old girl who she met at a UNICEF-supported nursery next to an Ebola treatment centre in Bunia, the Ituri capital. Lina’s mother died and her father is missing. Her grandfather, who lives nearby, has visited twice and the hope is that they will soon be together. Another child, Raphael*, just eight months old, survived Ebola but lost eight family members. He stayed at the nursery for more than three weeks until his older brother could take him home. Young lives lost “Children are not only losing their parents. They're also losing their own lives,” Ms. Amadou said. As of 29 September, at least 2,017 children had been confirmed with Ebola in DRC. At least 1,062 have died. She noted that children make up just over one in four confirmed cases, but around one in three deaths. However, the situation is worse among under-fives where the death rate is seven in 10, up from six in 10 just a few weeks ago. “Many die before the virus is ever detected, before they ever reach treatment,” she said. Care and access While in Bunia Ms. Amadou “also saw what works” for young lives upended by Ebola. UNICEF supports 12 nurseries in Ituri and North Kivyu that care for babies and young children who have been exposed to the virus, or whose parents are in treatment, or who are on their own. “Children are fed, they are held, they're cared for, they are also watched closely so that if symptoms appear, they get paediatric care fast,” she said. UNICEF is calling for nurseries at every Ebola treatment centre in the DRC, while underscoring the need to maintain health essential services. That way children receive early detection and quick referral to Ebola care, as well as protection from common childhood diseases. First case in Kenya Meanwhile, the World Health Organization (WHO) is monitoring the situation in Kenya, which on Tuesday confirmed its first case and fatality, according to media reports. Spokesman Christian Lindmeier the case was “likely imported from DRC” but more information was not available. He said colleagues on the ground are working with the Kenyan authorities to get more details. *Names have been changed to protect the children’s privacy and identity Ebola Virus Disease Facebook Twitter Print Email Back to top

news.title_zh: 联合国儿童基金会:“埃博拉夺走了儿童所依赖的人” - 联合国新闻
news.source_body_en: The UNICEF report, published on 6 October 2026, highlights the devastating impact of the Ebola outbreak in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on children. Since the outbreak was declared in May, over 1,900 children have either lost one or both parents or caregivers, with 1,581 in North Kivu and 322 in neighboring areas. As of 29 September, at least 2,017 children had been confirmed with Ebola, and 1,062 had died. Children under five face a particularly high risk, with a death rate of seven in 10. UNICEF is supporting nurseries in Ituri and North Kivu to care for affected children, emphasizing the need for early detection and treatment. Meanwhile, Kenya confirmed its first case and death from Ebola, likely imported from the DRC, with the WHO working to gather more information. The report underscores the emotional and logistical challenges faced by children during the outbreak.
news.content_zh: 联合国儿童基金会于 2026 年 10 月 6 日发布的报告强调了刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 东部埃博拉病毒 暴发 对儿童造成的破坏性影响。自 5 月宣布 暴发 以来,已有 1,900 多名儿童失去父母一方或双方或照顾者,其中 1,581 名儿童在北基伍省,322 名儿童在邻近地区。截至9月29日,至少有2,017名儿童被确诊感染埃博拉病毒,其中1,062人死亡。五岁以下儿童面临的风险特别高,死亡率为十分之七。联合国儿童基金会正在支持伊图里和北基伍省的托儿所照顾受影响的儿童,强调早期发现和 治疗 的必要性。与此同时,肯尼亚确认了首例埃博拉病例和死亡病例,很可能是从刚果民主共和国输入的,世界卫生组织正在努力收集更多信息。该报告强调了儿童在 暴发 期间面临的情感和后勤挑战。

supplementary_news.content: Research news 01 Oct, 2026 Researchers have developed a rapid approach to validate diagnostic tests for Bundibugyo virus and found evidence that an existing Zaire ebolavirus vaccine could provide cross-protection, offering potential tools to strengthen responses to the 2026 outbreak The current outbreak of Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has highlighted the difficulties that health authorities face when a rare and dangerous pathogen emerges for which dedicated diagnostic tests, vaccines and treatments are unavailable or at best limited. Two studies led by researchers from the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin and the German Primate Center – Leibniz Institute for Primate Research in Göttingen – including international collaborators – have examined different aspects of the response. The research assessed how diagnostic tests could be evaluated rapidly and whether an established Ebola vaccine might offer some protection against BDBV. During the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers at Charité led by Professor Christian Drosten, a DZIF scientist, rapidly developed a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay for Sars-CoV-2 virus. Its validated design was made publicly available which allowed manufacturers and laboratories to reproduce it and helped to expand testing capacity. European Union legislation has since introduced more stringent requirements for diagnostic devices. Although intended to ensure test performance, these requirements can present difficulties during outbreaks when validated diagnostics are required rapidly and appropriate reference materials are scarce. The 2026 BDBV outbreak provided an opportunity to address this problem. BDBV belongs to the Ebolavirus genus and can cause severe Ebola virus disease but there is no vaccine or therapeutic treatment specifically licensed against it. On 20 May 2026, the Charité hospital admitted a patient from the USA who had contracted BDBV in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Researchers obtained viral genetic material from a throat swab and established a reference standard against which candidate diagnostic assays could be evaluated. The team assembled an international network of nine laboratories that included DZIF members, the German National University Medicine Network (NUM), European research consortia, university hospitals and biosafety level four laboratories – the highest laboratory containment level. The network assessed four candidate PCR tests from two manufacturers. Within two weeks, the laboratories completed analytical and clinical evaluations, with no evidence of cross-reactivity. The results demonstrated that a decentralised network could rapidly generate robust test-performance data to support regulatory assessment and deployment during an infectious disease emergency. The researchers also highlighted the importance of collaboration between publicly funded laboratories and diagnostic manufacturers. Rare pathogens provide relatively little commercial incentive to develop tests that might be required only occasionally, so public investment would be required to maintain preparedness for high-consequence diseases. A second study, led by DZIF scientist Professor Stefan Pöhlmann at the German Primate Center, examined the biological characteristics of the 2026 BDBV strain and whether vaccination against Zaire ebolavirus might offer cross-protection. Researchers focused on the viral glycoprotein, a surface protein that allows ebolaviruses to enter host cells and represents an important target for neutralising antibodies. Because authentic BDBV requires biosafety level four containment, they used pseudovirus particles that carried glycoproteins from BDBV strains associated with outbreaks in 2007–08, 2012 and 2026. The experiments found no evidence that the 2026 glycoprotein allowed more efficient entry into human cells than those from earlier strains. Researchers also examined serum from ten healthy volunteers who had received the licensed recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus-Zaire ebolavirus vaccine, known as rVSV-ZEBOV. Samples were assessed before vaccination and at 28 and 180 days afterwards. After vaccination, antibodies could neutralise pseudoviruses that carried glycoproteins from all three BDBV strains. BDBV-specific neutralising activity was detected in six of the ten vaccine recipients at both post-vaccination time points, although activity was approximately 3.5 to 3.6 times lower than against Zaire ebolavirus. The results provide evidence that antibodies elicited by the licensed vaccine can recognise and inhibit BDBV in laboratory models. However, the researchers cautioned that the experiments did not demonstrate protection against BDBV infection or disease in people because the study used pseudoviruses and measured neutralisation in vitro. Taken together, the studies demonstrate how diagnostic science, virology and immunology can provide complementary tools during an infectious disease outbreak. International laboratory networks, accessible reference materials and regulatory mechanisms established before an emergency could help to reduce the interval between identification of an emerging pathogen and access to reliable diagnostics and potential preventive measures. supplementary_news.content_title: Kenya’s First Ebola Case Puts Contact Tracing to the Test
supplementary_news.content: Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale said the Ministry had identified 28 contacts. Officials are also tracing 23 passengers and four crew on Jambojet flight 8523. The groups reflect different checks: exposure at home or during care, and people who shared the journey. Authorities have not said how many have completed follow-up. The Ministry said the patient, who had lived in the DRC for seven years, fell ill about a month before returning. After treatment at several DRC facilities, he travelled by road to Kampala and flew to Nairobi on 3 October. He underwent routine screening at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, then was taken to Nairobi Hospital and isolated. Public accounts do not specify whether symptoms were evident at the airport, a detail needed to assess screening and referral without assuming a lapse. He later died despite supportive care. Authorities have not named him. Officials say 28 close contacts, including relatives and health workers, have been identified. Separately, authorities are tracing 23 passengers and four crew from the flight to Nairobi. These are response groups, not a count of infected people. The test is whether people at meaningful exposure risk can be located and monitored through the virus’s incubation period. Kenya’s first confirmed imported Ebola case has turned months of preparedness into a test of contact tracing and hospital infection control. The patient, a Kenyan returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), died late on 5 October after testing positive for Bundibugyo virus disease, the Health Ministry announced the next day. Porini Point is a large, phased apartment development planned within Tatu City, a 5,000-acre mixed-use city in Kiambu County. The development is designed as a low-rise residential community containing approximately 570 apartments across 24 ground-plus-four-storey blocks. The project offers one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments arranged around landscaped courtyards and shared recreational areas. Planned amenities include a residents’ clubhouse, swimming pool and sun deck, indoor and outdoor fitness facilities, barbecue area, children’s playground, landscaped gardens, resident and visitor parking, controlled access and security services. Porini Point is positioned close to Tatu City’s schools, offices, industrial and commercial districts, healthcare services, shops, restaurants and recreation facilities. The development is also marketed for its proximity to the planned 160-acre Tatu Wildlife Sanctuary. Apartments are sold unfurnished. Published specifications include SPC parquet-style flooring in living and bedroom areas, ceramic tiles in wet areas, quartz kitchen countertops, fitted cabinetry, open-plan kitchens, hob, oven, extractor hood, laundry areas, large windows and private balconies on upper-floor units. Selected ground-floor apartments may include private gardens. The official project information states that the first three buildings are targeted for handover in Q1 2027, while the complete development is targeted for Q4 2029. Buyers should obtain a unit-specific completion date and contractual long-stop date before committing funds. One-bedroom apartment — 54 m2 The one-bedroom apartment is designed for individuals, couples, corporate tenants and investors seeking a relatively accessible entry point into Tatu City. The published layout includes: Living and dining area. Open-plan fitted kitchen. Separate bedroom. Full bathroom. Laundry area. Private balcony on upper floors. One parking space. Best suited to: young professionals, returning diaspora, corporate tenants, first-time buyers and furnished-rental investors. Two-bedroom apartment — 90 m2 Two alternative two-bedroom layouts are offered. Both include a main bedroom with an ensuite bathroom, a second bedroom, separate shared bathroom, living and dining space, fitted kitchen, laundry area and balcony. Best suited to: couples, small families, professional house-sharers and medium- to long-term tenants. Three-bedroom apartment — 145 m2 The three-bedroom configuration offers larger living accommodation, three bathrooms, a walk-in wardrobe, laundry space and two balconies. Two parking spaces are included in the published price. Best suited to: families, owner-occupiers, senior professionals and buyers prioritising space over maximum rental yield. 7. Location breakdown Where is Porini Point located? Porini Point is located inside Tatu City, near Ruiru in Kiambu County, north of Nairobi. Tatu City is accessible through several regional road connections, including Thika Superhighway, the Eastern and Northern bypasses, Kiambu Road and Ruiru–Kiambu Road. The official project material estimates approximately: 30–35 minutes to Nairobi CBD under favourable conditions. 30–32 minutes to Westlands. Approximately 30 minutes to the United Nations area. 35–45 minutes to Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. Actual travel times vary significantly with traffic and the chosen route. Nearby schools Crawford International School. Nova Pioneer Primary School. Nova Pioneer High School. Planned and developing education facilities within Tatu City. Shopping, food and services Naivas supermarket. Cafés and restaurants within Tatu City. Banking facilities. Pharmacy and healthcare services. Safaricom and everyday retail services. Tatu City commercial and office districts. Employment and business districts Tatu Industrial Park. Tatu City Special Economic Zone. Tatu Central business district. Office and co-working facilities. More than 100 operating businesses across the wider city. Recreation and green spaces Tatu City walking and cycling trails. Parks and landscaped areas. Sports and outdoor fitness facilities. Planned Tatu Wildlife Sanctuary. Porini Point clubhouse, swimming pool and play areas. The wildlife sanctuary should be described as planned or under development, not as an already operational attraction. 8. Investment section Is Porini Point a good investment? Porini Point may appeal to investors seeking exposure to a master-planned development with schools, businesses, infrastructure and residential demand in one location. Its one-bedroom apartments offer the lowest entry price and potentially the broadest tenant pool, while larger units may attract families and long-term occupants. The developer’s published model estimates monthly rents of: Unit Unfurnished estimate Furnished estimate One bedroom KES 55,000 KES 95,000 Two bedroom KES 70,000 KES 130,000 Three bedroom KES 100,000 KES 160,000 These estimates generate advertised gross yields of approximately 7%–16% against the published cash prices. They are projections rather than guaranteed returns and exclude vacancy, tax, management fees, service charges, furnishing, maintenance and transaction costs. The 21-day period is the outer edge of WHO’s estimated incubation window, not a claim that an entire community is at risk. WHO says people are not contagious before symptoms begin; spread is through direct contact with blood or other bodily fluids, or materials contaminated by them. That is why named-contact tracing, infection control in care settings and safe burial are central to containment. The Ministry also reported 267 samples tested across five laboratories by 6 October, with one positive; 4,971 health workers trained; and 652,584 travellers screened. These figures describe capacity and workload, not whether every contact has been reached. Updates on follow-up and test results will be more useful than screening totals alone. Bundibugyo is not the Ebola strain many people know This case involves Bundibugyo virus, a distinct Ebola-causing virus with no approved specific treatment or vaccine. Licensed Ebola vaccines and antibody treatments target Zaire ebolavirus, not this strain. Supportive care remains available: WHO says early intensive care, including fluid replacement and treatment of symptoms, can improve survival. WHO says evidence that Ervebo, a Zaire-strain vaccine, offers meaningful protection against Bundibugyo in people is insufficient. Its 1 September guidance recommends possible use only under research protocols. So “there is an Ebola vaccine” is not accurate shorthand for protection against this outbreak’s virus. Bundibugyo’s early symptoms can resemble malaria and other illnesses, making laboratory confirmation important. WHO gives a two-to-21-day incubation period; people become infectious after symptoms begin. Spread occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials, and can be amplified by failures in health-care infection control or unsafe handling of bodies. This is why response hinges on triage, testing, follow-up and safe burial—not avoiding ordinary contact with every traveller. A regional outbreak, with a Kenyan test of preparedness Kenya’s Health Ministry links the case to a traveller returning from the DRC; his stop in Kampala does not make Uganda the source. WHO and Africa CDC declared Uganda’s Bundibugyo outbreak over on 27 August after 42 days without a confirmed case. The DRC outbreak remains active. WHO data through 3 October recorded 8,544 confirmed cases and 4,114 deaths there—figures not Kenyan cases and subject to revision. Kenya had prepared for importation. In September, WHO reported training for health workers and border stakeholders at Busia, Malaba and Lwakhakha, but also a staffing gap in night-time screening of small-scale traders at Busia. That was not this patient’s route; it shows why airport screening alone is not enough. Community alerts, after-hours coverage, laboratory turnaround and hospital infection control must connect. The confirmed case and death are serious, but one reported infection does not by itself show wider transmission in Kenya. The next indicators are whether the contacts and flight group are accounted for, anyone develops symptoms, and suspected cases are isolated and tested promptly. The Ministry directs the public to its official channels and toll-free line 719 for updates, and says people who are unwell should seek care at recognised facilities. Calm cooperation supports containment; stigma and speculation do not

Streamline Feed OfficialVerified Oct 2, 2026Updated Oct 2, 20264 min read Report article Follow on Google News Try askingWhy does this matter? Local SEO Leads Kenya (LSLK) 4.0(1) Nairobi Explore Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% The ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has claimed more than 4,000 lives, making it the fastest-growing and second-deadliest on record. Health authorities confirmed 4,018 deaths among 8,300 confirmed cases across seven provinces. Efforts to contain the virus are increasingly hampered by protests over unpaid wages among frontline responders and violent resistance within affected communities. The Ministry of Health, Hygiene and Social Welfare released the updated figures on Friday, underscoring the severity of the 17th Ebola epidemic to strike the Central African nation. Since the outbreak was officially declared on May 15, 2026, it has outpaced the transmission rate of all previous crises. The overall case fatality rate currently stands at 48.4 percent, with 2,162 patients having formally recovered. The World Health Organization declared the crisis a Public Health Emergency of International Concern shortly after its onset. The rapid spread into new health zones, stretching from the epicentres in Ituri and North Kivu provinces to remote regions, continues to strain limited national and international health resources. The Bundibugyo Strain Challenge Unlike the recent outbreaks in the region, the 2026 epidemic is driven by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus. The pathogen presents a distinct challenge because existing medical countermeasures, including the widely deployed rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine and specific antiviral treatments, were developed exclusively for the Zaire ebolavirus. Currently, there is no approved vaccine or recognised antiviral treatment for the Bundibugyo strain. This medical limitation forces health agencies to rely heavily on traditional public health interventions: aggressive contact tracing, isolation, strict infection prevention protocols, and supportive clinical care. The pace of transmission has been unprecedented. The 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo—previously the second-largest in history—took approximately 235 days to record 1,000 confirmed cases. The current epidemic surpassed the 1,000-case milestone within 40 days of response activation, fundamentally altering the baseline for epidemic forecasting in the region. Frontline Workers Demand Unpaid Wages The medical response has been severely disrupted by recurring administrative failures. In Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province and the heart of the outbreak, health workers gathered this week to demand months of owed wages. Surveillance team members, who hold the critical responsibility of finding and monitoring people who came into contact with infected patients, joined the protests. Demonstrators waved placards reading "No money, no data" and "No payment for months" before being dispersed by local officials. The strikes have created dangerous blind spots in the epidemiological data, preventing authorities from mapping the exact transmission chains. The occupational hazards for those engaged in the response remain extraordinarily high. An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières contracted the virus while working in the country. The worker was evacuated on a special medical flight to the Netherlands late Thursday night and transferred to a high-level isolation unit at the Leiden University Medical Center. Comparison of the Largest Ebola Outbreaks in History Outbreak Period Primary Location Ebolavirus Strain Confirmed Cases Recorded Deaths 2014–2016 West Africa Zaire 28,600+ 11,300+ May 2026–Present Democratic Republic of the Congo Bundibugyo 8,300 4,018 2018–2020 Democratic Republic of the Congo Zaire 3,470 2,280 Violent Community Resistance Public health interventions are also battling intense local resistance. Widespread mistrust of government officials and health workers, compounded by chronic insecurity and historical grievances, has frequently erupted into violence against response teams. Earlier this week, Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local politician with the ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, was beaten to death by a mob at his home in Butembo, North Kivu. He had been publicly defending the government's outbreak containment measures. Following the fatal assault, his house was set on fire. The incident highlights the severe tensions between the state apparatus and communities who often view the Ebola response with deep suspicion, with some residents continuing to dismiss the virus as a manufactured hoax. Last month, authorities attempted to pivot to a "village-centred approach," aimed at empowering local leaders to manage surveillance and isolation protocols. However, the assassination in Butembo underscores the limits of this strategy when foundational trust is absent. International Funding and Data Gaps The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention indicated during its latest briefing that while the number of newly confirmed cases appears to be falling in certain hotspots, this trend must be interpreted with caution. The apparent decline is likely driven by escalating insecurity and the breakdown of community cooperation, which prevents surveillance teams from accurately recording new infections. International funding is slowly adapting to the scale of the emergency. The Canadian government recently announced $36 million to support the Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and neighbouring Uganda. The funding is earmarked for public health operations, humanitarian assistance, and $4 million specifically directed toward the research and development of medical countermeasures for the Bundibugyo strain. Until targeted vaccines and therapeutics enter clinical trials, the trajectory of the outbreak remains entirely dependent on basic epidemiological control. With surveillance networks disrupted by strikes and violence, the true scale of the transmission network likely exceeds the official registry, leaving the timeline for containment entirely uncertain. Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% Outbreak Surpasses Grim Milestone Across Multiple Provinces Authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have confirmed that the ongoing Ebola outbreak has now caused more than 4,000 deaths, marking a devastating escalation in one of the most severe public health crises the region has faced in recent years [[16]]. The outbreak, driven by the Bundibugyo virus strain, has spread far beyond its initial epicenter, with cases confirmed across at least seven provinces, including Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, Bas-Uélé, and Sud-Ubangi [[85]]. Health officials report that the total number of confirmed cases has surpassed 8,000, resulting in a case fatality rate of approximately 50 percent [[24]]. The rapid geographic expansion of the virus has overwhelmed local health infrastructure, forcing the Ministry of Health and international partners to stretch their resources across a vast and often inaccessible terrain. The Bundibugyo virus, while historically less widespread than the Zaire ebolavirus, poses a severe threat due to its high mortality rate and the logistical challenges associated with deploying targeted vaccines and therapeutics in active conflict zones. Community Mistrust and Security Challenges Containment efforts have been severely hampered by deep-seated community mistrust and ongoing insecurity, particularly in the eastern provinces of North Kivu and Ituri [[91]]. In these regions, armed conflict and the presence of numerous militant groups frequently disrupt contact tracing, safe burial practices, and vaccination campaigns. Health workers operating in these hotspots often face hostility from local populations who view the medical response with suspicion, a dynamic that has historically allowed the virus to spread undetected through remote communities. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) and other frontline organizations have been forced to adapt their strategies, focusing on community engagement and decentralized care to bypass security roadblocks [[87]]. As part of the Ministry of Health-led response, MSF is currently conducting a major study following 20,000 frontline workers in Ituri and North Kivu to better understand the occupational hazards and transmission vectors within medical facilities [[87]]. Despite these efforts, the shortage of trained personnel and essential medical supplies remains a critical bottleneck, leaving many rural health centers ill-equipped to isolate suspected cases or manage severe hemorrhagic symptoms. International Response and Vaccine Limitations The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) have mobilized emergency response teams to support the DRC government, but the scale of the outbreak continues to outpace the available resources [[24]]. Unlike previous outbreaks driven by the Zaire ebolavirus, which can be targeted with the highly effective rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine, the Bundibugyo strain requires different medical countermeasures that are currently in shorter supply. This biological distinction has complicated ring vaccination strategies, forcing health authorities to rely heavily on strict isolation protocols and intensive surveillance to break chains of transmission. The international community has been urged to increase financial and logistical support, as the outbreak threatens to destabilize an already fragile region. Neighboring countries, including Uganda, which has also experienced recent Ebola incidents, remain on high alert, implementing rigorous cross-border screening measures to prevent the virus from spreading internationally [[84]]. As the death toll climbs, the DRC's struggle to contain the Bundibugyo virus underscores the persistent vulnerability of conflict-affected regions to zoonotic diseases and the urgent need for more versatile, broadly effective vaccine platforms. Historical Context of DRC's Ebola Battles The Democratic Republic of Congo has a long and tragic history with the Ebola virus, having recorded its first outbreak in 1976 near the Ebola River [[93]]. This current crisis represents the country's 15th recorded epidemic, but it is distinguished by its unprecedented geographic reach and the involvement of the Bundibugyo species [[93]]. Historically, outbreaks in the DRC were confined to remote, heavily forested areas in the northwest, such as Equateur province, where containment was easier to manage due to lower population density and limited mobility [[93]]. The shift toward the densely populated and highly mobile eastern provinces has fundamentally altered the epidemiology of the disease. Urban centers and busy transit corridors in North Kivu and Ituri facilitate rapid transmission, making traditional quarantine measures far more difficult to enforce. Health experts note that the intersection of high population mobility, porous borders, and chronic underinvestment in rural healthcare has created a perfect storm for the virus, turning what might have been a localized event into a protracted national emergency. supplementary_news.content_title: NanoViricides Advances Phase II Trial of Oral Ebola Treatment as Congo Outbreak Continues
supplementary_news.content: NanoViricides, Inc. (NYSE American: NNVC), a clinical-stage antiviral drug developer, has provided an update on its Phase II clinical trial of NV-387 Oral Gummies for the treatment of Bundibugyo Ebolavirus (BDBV) and other Ebola viruses in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The trial is proceeding as designed, with enrollment in Phase IIA beginning on or about Sept. 23, 2026. Phase IIA is intended to identify an optimal, well-tolerated dosing regimen and serve as a go/no-go step before Phase IIB, a randomized controlled trial designed to evaluate efficacy. The company said NV-387 is designed to attack the virus and reduce viral load and is delivered as an oral gummy that dissolves in the mouth without requiring water or swallowing effort. If successful, the oral treatment could be readily deployed in resource-limited settings, where traditional injectable Ebola therapies may be difficult to administer. NanoViricides characterized NV-387 as a broad-spectrum antiviral that mimics a host-side feature used by Ebola viruses and said there is a rationale for potential activity against Bundibugyo and other Ebola viruses. For full details, see the company’s press release . The news matters because the ongoing Bundibugyo outbreak in the DRC highlights the need for easy-to-use therapeutics that can be deployed rapidly in remote areas. An oral gummy that does not require refrigeration or trained personnel for administration could significantly improve outbreak response. NanoViricides, Inc. (NYSE American: NNVC) is a clinical-stage company creating special purpose nanomaterials for antiviral therapy. Its novel nanoviricideTM class of drug candidates is based on intellectual property and technology from TheraCour Pharma, Inc. Beyond Ebola, NV-387 is being developed as a broad-spectrum antiviral for RSV, COVID, Long COVID, Influenza, and other respiratory viral infections, as well as MPOX/Smallpox and Measles. The company’s other advanced candidate is NV-HHV-1 for Shingles. NanoViricides holds a worldwide exclusive perpetual license to TheraCour’s nanomedicine technology for several human viral diseases, including HIV/AIDS, Hepatitis B and C, Rabies, Herpes, Influenza, Dengue, and Ebola/Marburg viruses. The company’s progress with NV-387 could position it as a key player in pandemic preparedness and response. However, as is customary in drug development, the path to approval is lengthy and requires substantial capital, and there can be no assurance that any candidate will show sufficient effectiveness and safety for human clinical development. The latest updates relating to NNVC are available in the company’s newsroom at https://ibn.fm/NNVC . Photo: WHO/Ardo Farah #Ethiopia UN relief chief calls for safe, rapid access as teams work to deliver life-saving help The Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, Tom Fletcher, said in a social media post that in northern Ethiopia, “our teams are working to get life-saving food, health and other help to people in need.” He called on all parties to give aid workers safe and rapid access. Meanwhile, ongoing hostilities continue to displace people across Central, North-Western and Eastern Tigray, although verified figures remain unavailable. The UN and its partners are prepared to resume aid operations in the northern regions, including Tigray, as and when they gain access. In the Amhara region, a Government-led effort to help people displaced by recent insecurity from the town of Kobo to their areas of origin was suspended following a deterioration in the security situation. The UN reiterates that any returns must be safe, voluntary, informed and dignified. #Ebola outbreak Democratic Republic of the Congo: UN, partners support scale-up of Ebola response The Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) says that the UN and its partners continue to support authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in scaling up the response to the Ebola outbreak. As of 3 October, authorities had reported more than 8,500 confirmed cases and over 4,100 deaths. Transmission has accelerated in recent days, with 102 new confirmed cases reported on 3 October, compared with 66 the previous day. The provinces of Ituri and North Kivu accounted for more than 94 per cent of the new cases. North Kivu remains among the hardest hit. Contact tracing coverage stands at just under 68 per cent – well below the target of 95 per cent – complicating efforts to break chains of transmission. The UN and its partners are also concerned about movement restrictions introduced yesterday along several key roads in North Kivu as part of efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak. While intended to curb transmission, these measures could further constrain humanitarian access, the movement of aid workers, and the continuity of response operations in some locations. Meanwhile, in the provinces of Haut-Uélé and Ituri, OCHA continues to support the Government’s efforts to strengthen Ebola prevention and surveillance in high-risk mining communities. Kenya: first imported case of Ebola confirmed The Government of Kenya has confirmed the country’s first imported case of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus. Kenyan authorities rapidly identified, isolated and tested the case, and response measures – including contact tracing, enhanced surveillance and public health monitoring – are already under way. The case underscores the regional risk, as transmission continues in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The UN’s message is clear: the response must continue until transmission is stopped, alongside cross-border surveillance, regional coordination, preparedness and readiness. The World Health Organization and its partners are supporting Kenya’s Ministry of Health and National Public Health Institute in preparedness and response efforts. Isolation units across 27 high-risk counties have been identified, and Ebola surveillance tools have been updated so that suspected cases can be quickly identified, reported and investigated. The UN and its partners are supporting Government-led efforts to prevent further transmission, strengthen preparedness and response capacities, and ensure a coordinated regional response. The UN continues to encourage countries across the region to strengthen cross-border surveillance, screening at points of entry, contact tracing and coordination to detect and respond rapidly to cases. #Occupied Palestinian Territory Gaza: funding gaps, supply restrictions hamper water, sanitation support OCHA says that support for water and sanitation in Gaza is being held back by funding shortfalls and restrictions on the entry of critical supplies.* Items subject to import restrictions include engine oil, spare parts and equipment critical to keep vehicles and machines running. Partners say that shortages have caused a decline in water production at two desalination plants in southern Gaza, where equipment could not be properly maintained. This has resulted in a slight reduction in drinking water for roughly 500,000 people in Deir al Balah and Khan Younis. Across Gaza, partners estimate that three in every four families rely on water delivered by truck, until water infrastructure can be fully restored. Partners are delivering 25,000 cubic metres of drinking water every day through 3,200 collection points. However, the vehicles they use need maintenance – and access to certain areas is often suspended due to insecurity, particularly along the so-called “Yellow Line.” In the fourth week of September, partners distributed over 12,000 water containers with a 10-litre capacity each to help people collect water distributed by truck. Partners also provided thousands of trash cans, bags, sponges and dusters; 3,000 litres of dishwashing soap; 4,600 gloves and facemasks; nearly 1,300 litres of bleach; over 200 latrines; and hundreds of hygiene kits. Recently, shortages of import-restricted items have prevented the use of vehicles to collect and transfer solid waste, forcing reliance on donkey carts and UN trucks instead. In addition to approvals for restricted items, access must be restored to Gaza’s two landfills that are close to the Strip’s perimeter to prevent further accumulation of solid waste in populated areas. Sustained funding for fuel is also critical. West Bank: scores of Palestinians displaced after building demolished in East Jerusalem Humanitarian partners say that 69 Palestinians, over half of them children, were displaced in the West Bank today after Israeli authorities demolished their residential building in At Tur area of East Jerusalem. This is the highest number of people displaced in a single demolition in East Jerusalem since UN records began in 2009. The UN and its partners visited the area, and families there said that Israeli forces had prevented them from retrieving their belongings, which were left buried under the rubble. Partners assessed people’s immediate humanitarian needs and made sure they can receive rent support and essential items. So far this year, Israeli authorities have demolished or forced owners to demolish the homes of more than 1,800 Palestinians across the West Bank. Most were demolished for lacking Israeli-issued building permits, which are rarely granted to Palestinians in the affected areas. Humanitarian partners have provided them with emergency shelter, essential items and psychosocial support. *Donations made to UN Crisis Relief help UN agencies and humanitarian NGOs reach people in the Occupied Palestinian Territory with urgent support
