Her work has previously appeared in Billboard and Reader's Digest. People Editorial Guidelines Published on October 6, 2026 01:31PM EDT Leave a Comment Add Us On Health workers in Mongbwalu, Democratic Republic of Congo, amid the Ebola outbreak in May 2026. Credit : Michel Lunanga/Getty NEED TO KNOW A Kenyan resident living in Congo flew to Nairobi, where he tested positive for Ebola Officials identified 55 contacts who will remain isolated for 21 days and receive testing The ongoing outbreak has sickened 8,442 people and is now the second largest Ebola outbreak on record Kenya officials have confirmed the first-ever case of Ebola in the country amid an ongoing outbreak of the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo. A Kenyan citizen residing in Congo had been ill for a month, and was treated in “several hospitals” in Congo, Kenya Health Minister Aden Duale said in an Oct. 6 press conference, per Reuters. The man traveled by road to Kampala, Uganda’s capital and, from there, flew on Oct. 3 to Nairobi, Kenya, on Jambojet Flight 8523, Duale said. Duale said that when the man arrived, he underwent the “normal public health screenings” but passed them. It’s the country’s first-ever case of Ebola, the BBC says. Ebola virus. Getty “We believe that the patient knew that he was already ill,” Health Ministry Director General Patrick Amoth said, saying that the treatment he had in Congo may have been “able to mask some of the symptoms,” which is why he passed the mandated health screening when he arrived at Nairobi International Airport. A relative took the patient from the airport directly to Nairobi Hospital, where he was admitted with fever, chills and bleeding beneath the skin. There, he tested positive for Ebola, Associated Press reports. The man was placed in isolation and given “supportive treatment”, but died on October 5. Related Stories American Doctor Exposed to Ebola Said Giving His Son a Smartphone "Feels Riskier Than What We’re Doing in Congo" The Largest Ebola Outbreak Sent the World Into a Panic 12 Years Ago. The Current Outbreak Could Surpass It Our new app is here! Free, fun and full of exclusives. Scan to download now! Officials have identified 28 people who were in contact with the man — including health care workers and family members — as well as 23 passengers who were on the flight, and four crew members. Amoth said the contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days, and after testing negative for the virus, they can be released. The disease is not considered to be airborne, and is not thought to be particularly contagious; however, it is infectious — meaning, it takes a small amount of contact with the virus to contract Ebola. The current outbreak of Ebola has sickened a confirmed 8,442 people, and killed 4,080, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. It’s now the second largest outbreak of Ebola on record, per the U.S. Centers for Disease Control, which adds that it “spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks.” The patient died at Nairobi Hospital on Oct. 5. Credit: OutofAfrica / WPietsch / Alamy Stock Photo Subscribe to PEOPLE magazine to get the news, how-it-happened true crime stories and more — right to your mailbox. Ebola is caused by a collection of viruses called orthoebolaviruses. The Bundibugyo strain is a relatively rare strain of the virus, as NPR reports, and isn’t always included in standard testing for Ebola. This may have led to delays in identifying early Ebola cases in this outbreak. According to the CDC, someone infected with Ebola doesn’t spread the disease until they’re symptomatic. Symptoms can appear as late as 21 days after contact with an infected person, and begin with what are called “dry” symptoms of Ebola, like fever, joint and muscle pain, headaches and fatigue. The disease then progresses to the “wet” symptoms, which, along with vomiting and diarrhea, include bleeding from the eyes, mouth, nose and rectum. The virus spreads through contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person — alive or dead. But Johns Hopkins Medicine explains, it can also spread by touching items, like clothing or bedsheets, that have been in contact with body fluids. In response, the World Health Organization has outlined stringent guidelines for disinfecting and disposing of anything that’s been in contact with an infected person. Authorities said that the Kenyan man will be buried within 24 hours, according to the safety protocols. Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% Kenya has confirmed its first imported case of the Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease, triggering a rapid multi-agency public health response after a passenger travelling from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) died shortly after arriving in Nairobi. Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale announced the development, detailing the patient's complex travel route and the immediate containment measures activated at the country's points of entry. The deceased, a Kenyan citizen who had been residing in the DRC, travelled by road to Kampala, Uganda, before boarding a Jambojet commercial flight to Nairobi. The passenger arrived on Jambojet flight JM8523 from Entebbe on October 3 and subsequently tested positive for the virus at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI). The patient later succumbed to the disease, marking a critical moment for Kenya's epidemiological surveillance systems. Aggressive Contact Tracing and Isolation In response to the confirmed case, the Ministry of Health has launched an aggressive contact tracing operation to identify and monitor anyone who may have been exposed to the virus. Authorities have already identified and isolated twenty-eight primary contacts, including family members and the healthcare workers who attended to the patient upon arrival. These individuals are currently under strict medical surveillance and monitoring for any symptoms of the disease. Furthermore, health officials are actively pursuing an additional twenty-three passengers and four crew members who were aboard the same Jambojet flight. The airline has stated that it is working in close coordination with the Ministry of Health, Port Health Services, and other relevant aviation and public health authorities to trace these individuals and ensure they are placed under the necessary observation protocols. The rapid identification of these contacts is considered the most critical step in preventing any potential local transmission. Understanding the Bundibugyo Strain The Bundibugyo ebolavirus is one of the four species of Ebola virus known to cause severe disease in humans. While it is generally associated with a lower case fatality rate compared to the more notorious Zaire ebolavirus strain, it remains a highly dangerous pathogen that requires immediate and rigorous containment. The virus is primarily transmitted through direct contact with the blood, bodily fluids, or contaminated surfaces of an infected person who is showing symptoms. Public health experts emphasize that Ebola is not an airborne disease and is not spread by individuals who are infected but asymptomatic. This biological reality means that the risk to the general public remains low, provided that the identified contacts are properly managed and isolated. The Ministry of Health has reassured the public that the national health system is well-prepared, drawing on extensive experience from previous regional outbreaks and routine preparedness drills conducted at major entry points like Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. Aviation and Border Security Protocols The incident has highlighted the critical importance of robust screening protocols at regional transit hubs. Because the patient transited through Uganda before entering Kenya, the case underscores the porous nature of regional borders and the necessity for seamless information sharing between neighboring states. Kenyan authorities are currently reviewing the thermal screening and health declaration forms utilized at the Entebbe and Nairobi airports to identify any potential gaps in the initial detection process. Jambojet, as the carrier involved, has faced intense scrutiny regarding its in-flight health protocols and the training of its cabin crew to recognize and manage medical emergencies involving infectious diseases. The airline's swift cooperation with health authorities is vital for ensuring that all potential exposure points within the aircraft are properly sanitized and that the manifest is accurately utilized for contact tracing. Aviation regulators are expected to issue updated advisories to all carriers operating within the East African Community. Regional Surveillance and Public Guidance Kenya has not previously reported a confirmed local outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain, though the country has maintained enhanced surveillance at all points of entry due to recurrent outbreaks in neighboring Central and East African nations. The Ministry of Health has urged citizens to remain calm but vigilant, advising the public to avoid contact with wild animals, practice rigorous hand hygiene, and immediately report any symptoms such as sudden fever, muscle pain, or unexplained bleeding to the nearest health facility. The World Health Organization (WHO) and other international health bodies are being kept abreast of the situation, providing technical support and monitoring the response to ensure it aligns with global health regulations. As the twenty-one-day incubation period for the identified contacts progresses, the success of Kenya's containment strategy will depend entirely on the strict adherence to isolation protocols and the continued vigilance of both the medical community and the traveling public. Add to preferred sources Comments News Lauren Edwards 11:07, 06 Oct 2026Updated 11:08, 06 Oct 2026 Kenya has confirmed its first case of Ebola(Image: AFP via Getty Images) The deadly 'bleeding-eye virus' known as Ebola is feared to be spreading after a man died shortly after boarding a flight. The patient was a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo for seven years before he returned to Kenya on Saturday. ‌ ‌ He had fallen ill about a month earlier and received treatment in several hospitals in the DR Congo. Kenyan Cabinet Secretary of Health Aden Duale said the patient boarded a flight back to the Kenya capital on Saturday. ‌ After arriving at the main airport the patient underwent normal public screening before they were transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city. The tests confirmed the patient was positive for the Ebola Bundibugyo virus, a rare strain of the deadly disease with no treatment. ‌ Kenyan Cabinet Secretary of Health Aden Duale said the patient travelled to Kenya on Saturday(Image: AFP via Getty Images) After being transferred to the hospital, it was reported the patient "developed fever, chills, intense fatigue and weakness, painful swallowing, muscle pain and bleeding under the skin". "Doctors suspected a viral haemorrhagic fever based on his symptoms and travel history and collected samples for testing. The sample tested positive for Ebola Bundibugyo virus," Duale said. So far, 28 contacts have been identified including family members and health workers. 4,000 people have died following the outbreak(Image: AFP via Getty Images) The current Ebola outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, and there are currently no approved vaccines or treatments, which is rare and highly infectious. Article continues below More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, with more than 8,000 cases, and it is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease. The outbreak earlier spread to Uganda, which reported 20 cases and two deaths, but the World Health Organization declared Uganda free of the disease in August. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, living or dead. It can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the disease, the Reuters news agency notes. Congo announced an outbreak on May 15, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine. Medical workers work inside a mobile lab set up to test rapidly for the Ebola virus in Butembo, Congo, on Sept. 30, 2026. AP Photo / Sebastien Kitsa Musayi Some health workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the heart of the outbreak, to demand payment for owed wages. They were quickly dispersed by officials. The protesting workers included surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients. They waved placards saying, "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months." Front-line workers have gone on several strikes since the start of the outbreak to demand payment, further hampering efforts to contain the disease. An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement. The worker arrived late Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement. "The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said. More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus. The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots. A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources. The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries. Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak. Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption. An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement. The worker arrived late Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement. "The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said. More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus. The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots. A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources. The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries. Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak. Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.
